muixeranga.name: Muixeranga
muixeranga.tagline: A traditional Valencian performance of street dance and figurative human towers.
muixeranga.profile: The Muixeranga is a collective tradition of street dance and human towers originating in the Kingdom of Valencia, Spain, and preserved primarily in the town of Algemesí. It combines acrobatic, choreographic, and religious elements, serving as a foundational ancestor to the modern Catalan castells. Unlike competitive human towers, the Muixeranga focuses on the creation of complex, symbolic plastic figures during the annual Mare de Déu de la Salut festival.
muixeranga.insight: The Muixeranga is a living, plastic choreography where human towers are not built for height, but to create symbolic, figurative scenes honoring the Virgin of Health.
sources: Source: Muixeranga on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muixeranga
muixeranga.profile_long:
The Muixeranga is a multifaceted tradition centered in the town of Algemesí, where it is performed annually on September 7 and 8 during the festival of the Mare de Déu de la Salut (Virgin of Health). Historically, the tradition was linked to local guilds, such as construction workers, who performed these dances as part of the town's religious processions. While the tradition dates back centuries, with roots potentially reaching the 13th century, the first concrete written record of its participation in the festival appears in the town's account books in 1733, when a stipend was paid to the musicians. By the mid-20th century, the tradition had nearly vanished, but it was successfully revived in 1973 through the efforts of local organizers and the formation of the 'Amics de la Muixeranga'.

At the heart of the Muixeranga is the performance of 'plastic' figures—human towers and tableaux that represent Marian symbols and other figurative shapes. The performance begins with the muixeranguers dancing in two rows, often carrying candles, accompanied by the hypnotic, ancient melodies of the tabalet (drum) and the dolçaina (shawm). The towers are built with a focus on technical complexity and symbolic representation rather than sheer height. A child, known as the 'enxaneta', traditionally tops the tower with open arms. The performers, who now number around 200, come from diverse professional backgrounds, though they are expected to possess strength and physical skill. The master of the group, or 'mestre', coordinates the choreography, trains new members, and directs the construction of the towers.

The costume is a distinct visual marker of the tradition, consisting of a shirt, trousers, and farmer's shoes, often featuring vertical red and blue stripes on a white base. This 'harlequin' appearance is said to have originated from the use of old mattress fabric. Beyond its aesthetic and acrobatic value, the Muixeranga is deeply embedded in the community's identity. It has been recognized by UNESCO as part of the intangible heritage of humanity, reflecting its role in maintaining local culture and social cohesion. Today, the tradition has expanded beyond Algemesí, with numerous 'Noves Muixerangues' (new groups) forming across the Valencian region, ensuring the survival of this ancient, symbolic art form.

furlana.name: Furlana
furlana.tagline: Italy — The furlana (also spelled furlane, forlane, friulana, forlana) is an Italian folk dance from the Italian re…
furlana.profile: The furlana (also spelled furlane, forlane, friulana, forlana) is an Italian folk dance from the Italian region of Friuli-Venezia Giulia. In Friulian, furlane means Friulian, in this case Friulian Dance. In Friuli there has been a Slav minority since the Slavic settlement of the Eastern Alps, and the furlana may well have originated as a Slavonic dance.
furlana.insight: It was introduced to France by André Campra in 1697 (in L'Europe galante) and 1699 (in Le carnaval de Venise, in which the first of two furlanas serves as a dance entry for a troupe of Slavs, Armenians, and Gypsies), and it quickly became a popular theatre and social dance there.

irish-dance.name: Irish dance
irish-dance.era: Traditional; competitive stepdance codified late 19th-20th c.; globalized 1994 (Riverdance)
irish-dance.tagline: Umbrella of Irish stepdance, ceili and set dancing.
irish-dance.profile: Irish dance is a group of traditional dance forms originating in Ireland, broadly divided into social dances (ceili and set dancing) and performance/solo dances (stepdance) (Wikipedia). Modern competitive stepdance is characterized by a rigid upper body and intricate, fast footwork in soft shoes (ghillies) or hard shoes; other solo forms include sean-nos (relaxed, close-to-the-floor, improvised) and festival dance. Ceili dancing is performed by groups of 2-16 to reels, jigs and hornpipes; the 30 standardized ceili dances appear in CLRG's official handbook 'Ar Rinci Ceili.' Set dances derive from French quadrilles for four couples. Accompaniment is Irish traditional music - fiddle, bodhran, concertina, flute, whistle. The form was globally popularized by Riverdance (1994).
irish-dance.insight: Irish group dancing was particularly influenced by the French quadrille in the late 18th century - a genuine France connection, but the tradition is unambiguously Irish, so the catalog's France label is a mislabel (Wikipedia).

hop-tu-naa.profile: Hop-tu-naa is a traditional Manx dance connected to the hop-tu-naa festivities around 31 October in the Isle of Man. lezginka.tagline: The Caucasus — Dagestan, Chechnya, Georgia, Azerbaijan. The fast warrior dance that crosses borders.
lezginka.profile: The Lezginka (Russian: Лезгинка) is a folk dance common throughout the North Caucasus. It is named after the Lezgin people. It uses a fast 68 rhythm, and can be either a solo male or a pair dance. According to Encyclopædia Britannica: Lezginka, also spelled Lezghinka, folk dance originating among the Lezgin people of the North Caucasus. It is a male solo dance (often with a sword) and also a couple dance. The man, imitating the eagle, falls to his knees, leaps up, and dances with concise steps and strong, sharp arm and body movements.
lezginka.insight: The dance has also been adapted into classical music in Aram Khachaturian's 1942 ballet Gayane.

odzemek.name: Odzemek
odzemek.tagline: A Slovak men's solo dance erupting from slow footwork into a fiery shepherd's axe duel.
odzemek.profile: The odzemok is a traditional Slovak and Moravian Wallachian solo dance for men characterized by improvisation, a gradual acceleration, and the use of a shepherd's axe called a valaška. Dancers begin with subtle footwork close to the ground, reflecting the name derived from 'od zeme,' before escalating into dramatic leaps, squat movements, and mock duels. It is accompanied by strings, cimbalom, fujara, and koncovka, inspiring classical works such as Dvořák's Slavonic Dances.
odzemek.insight: In 1886, Antonín Dvořák immortalized the accelerating rhythms of the odzemek as the opening piece of his Slavonic Dances Op. 72.

odzemek.profile_long:
The odzemok is a traditional solo dance for men originating in Slovakia and Moravian Wallachia. Its name derives from the phrase 'od zeme,' translating directly to 'from the ground,' which describes the intimate relationship between the dancer's feet and the earth during the opening moments of the performance. Historically practised as an improvised male dance, it has also served as inspiration for classical European art music, most notably when Antonín Dvořák composed the opening piece of his Slavonic Dances Op. 72 based on its distinct energetic arc.

The dance begins with subtle foot movements close to the floor that gradually become more dramatic and fast-paced. Dancers maintain an improvised character throughout, sometimes incorporating elements reminiscent of eastern squat dances or the Ukrainian hopak. When performed in a large group setting, two dancers will separate from the ensemble and come together to execute a dynamic mock duel. This confrontation features athletic jumping and ducking maneuvers, where one participant directs movements toward the head while the other targets the lower legs. In most regions, performers handle a traditional shepherd's axe known as a valaška, though certain Eastern Slovak localities substitute a long wooden stick.

Musical accompaniment is provided by background ensembles typical of traditional Moravian and Slovak configurations. These groups prominently feature string instruments paired with the cimbalom, creating a rhythmic and harmonic foundation that matches the dance's acceleration. In addition to strings and cimbalom, musicians frequently utilize traditional wind instruments such as the fujara and the koncovka to enrich the acoustic landscape.

The dance serves as a vibrant expression of traditional male bravado and physical agility, historically anchored in the cultural practices of Slovakia and Moravian Wallachia through both solo improvisation and structured group mock duels. Composer Antonín Dvořák stands out as a notable figure who engaged with the tradition, utilizing the odzemek form to shape the first piece of his renowned Slavonic Dances Op. 72. Regional variations span across Slovakia and Moravian Wallachia, with specific distinctions noted in prop usage: while the valaška shepherd's axe is standard in most regions, Eastern Slovak areas frequently employ a long stick instead. The dance shares stylistic kinships and comparative elements with eastern squat dances and the Ukrainian hopak, while its musical lineage extends into 19th-century classical compositions.

jig.profile: The jig (Irish: port, Scottish Gaelic: port-cruinn) is a form of lively folk dance in compound metre, as well as the accompanying dance tune. It first gained popularity across the British Isles in the 16th-century, and was adopted on mainland Europe where it eventually became the final movement of the mature Baroque dance suite (the French gigue; Italian and Spanish giga). It is most associated with Irish dance music, Scottish country dance, French Canadian traditional music and dance and the Métis people in Canada.
jig.insight: It is second in popularity only to the reel in traditional Irish dance, and in Scottish country dance jigs and reels are the two quicktime dance forms.

kolo.tagline: The Slavic circle dance — opens every Serbian wedding, closes every village festival.
kolo.profile: Kolo (Serbian Cyrillic: Коло) is a South Slavic circle dance, found under this name in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, and Serbia. It is inscribed on the UNESCO List of Intangible Cultural Heritage for Serbia.
kolo.insight: UNESCO inscribed Serbia's Kolo on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2017 — recognising not just the dance but the social fabric it carries. Tradition holds that whoever joins the kolo is welcomed regardless of standing, age, or origin; the circle is intentionally non-hierarchical, and the dancer who leads (the kolovođa) is chosen by collective decision rather than rank.

karsilamas.name: Karsilamas
karsilamas.tagline: Greek-Turkish 'facing dance' in 9/8 time — the limping rhythm of the Anatolian wedding floor.
karsilamas.profile: Karsilamas (Turkish: karşılama; Greek: καρσιλαμάς) is a folk dance spread all over Northwest Turkey and carried to Greece by Anatolian Greek immigrants. The term "karşılama" means "encounter, welcoming, greeting" in Turkish. The dance is popular in Northwestern areas of Turkey, especially on wedding parties and festivals. This dance is also found in many areas of Greece, such as the Aegean islands (Syros, Kythnos, Lesvos, etc.) as well as in Thrace and Macedonia. Apart from Karsilamas, in Greece and Cyprus there is a similar dance named Antikrystos.
karsilamas.insight: Karsilamas's 9/8 time signature — the 'limping' 2+2+2+3 count — connects it to a vast Anatolian rhythmic family that includes Bulgaria's kopanitsa, Macedonia's lesnoto, and Ottoman-era court music; the same off-balance feel appears in dance forms from Albania to Armenia. Pontic Greek diaspora carried karsilamas from the Black Sea coast to Greek communities worldwide after the the early-20th-century Greek-Turkish population exchange.

perinia.profile: Perinița (or Pernița) is a traditional Romanian wedding folk dance. The dance is typical in the Muntenia region. The dance consists of participants forming a circle with one of the participants holding a handkerchief (or pillow) while dancing inside the circle. A circle of unmarried young people dance and accept him on the day before the marriage of one of the girls and it should be the last partner dance in which they will participate. One of the guys goes out in the dance inside the circle, holding a handkerchief.

qaytarma.name: Qaytarma
qaytarma.tagline: A cyclical Crimean Tatar folk dance defined by its 'returning' motion.
qaytarma.profile: Qaytarma, meaning 'returning,' is a traditional Crimean Tatar dance and musical form characterized by cyclical, rotational movements. It is performed by Crimean Tatars, Krymchaks, Crimean Karaites, Urums, and Ukrainian Greeks, primarily at weddings and holidays. The dance features distinct roles for men and women, with male dancers performing sharp, jumpy movements and female dancers emphasizing smooth, fluid gestures. It remains a living tradition, deeply embedded in the cultural identity of the Crimean Peninsula and surrounding regions.
qaytarma.insight: In 1903, composer Alexander Spendiaryan transcribed Qaytarma music in Bilohirsk, marking the first written record of a tradition that researchers recorded in 25 distinct versions by 1925.
sources: Source: Qaytarma on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qaytarma

video_stack.title: Qirim Ailesi - Ağır Ava ve Qaytarma

qaytarma.profile_long: Qaytarma, also known as Haytarma, is a foundational element of Crimean Tatar cultural expression. The name itself, which translates to 'returning,' reflects the cyclical nature of the movement and the music. Historically, the dance has been a staple of social life, performed during weddings and various community holidays. While its exact origins are a subject of academic debate, the dance has been documented as far back as 1793. Researchers have proposed various theories regarding its development, including connections to Sufi whirling traditions or potential influences from Sephardic Jewish populations arriving in Crimea after their expulsion from the Iberian Peninsula. Despite these theories, ethnographic work, such as that conducted by Asan Refatov in 1932, has argued for the unique, indigenous nature of the dance, suggesting it developed independently of Russian, Turkish, or Iranian cultural influences. The dance is not exclusive to Crimean Tatars; it is also practiced by Krymchaks, Crimean Karaites, Urums, and Ukrainian Greeks, with regional variations documented as far as the south-eastern Pryazovia region. The 1925 ethnographic expedition led by Usein Bodaninsky, Osman Aqçoqraqlı, and Asan Refatov was a watershed moment, identifying 25 distinct versions of the dance. This diversity highlights the adaptability and widespread nature of the tradition across different communities. In the 20th century, the dance transitioned into the public and artistic spheres. The establishment of the Qaytarma ensemble in 1939 as part of the Crimean State Philharmonic helped institutionalize the performance of the dance. Its presence in popular culture is significant, ranging from Alexander Spendiaryan’s 1903 musical transcription to Ennan Alimov’s 1930s painting, 'Girl Dancing Qaytarma.' More recently, the dance has been featured in contemporary media, such as the 2013 film 'Haytarma' by Akhtem Seitablayev, and was commemorated on a 2015 postage stamp issued by Ukrposhta. The dance remains a living tradition, serving as a vital link to the history and identity of the Crimean Tatar people and their neighbors.

pontic-greek-folk-dance.name: Pontic Greek Folk Dance
pontic-greek-folk-dance.tagline: Pontic Greek dance — Black Sea Greeks' tradition carried in diaspora after 1923, played in driving 9/8 and 5/8 time.
pontic-greek-folk-dance.profile: Pontic Greek folk dances are a group of over ninety dances traditionally performed by Pontic Greeks (Pontic: Ρωμαίοι). Dance has been an integral part of Pontian culture since ancient times. Dances vary based on region. Today, few Pontians remain in the Pontus region, but those living in the diaspora worldwide still perform folk dances to preserve their cultural heritage and group identity. Dances are accompanied by traditional music. Some traditional instruments include the lyra, daouli, zurna, dankiyo, tulum, and oud. The instrumental music may or may not be accompanied by singing.
pontic-greek-folk-dance.insight: In addition, dancers performed Pontian dances at the closing of the 2004 Olympic Games in Athens. Mouzenidis, writing for the Greek periodical Pontiaki Estia in 1956, argued that the serra represents a fight almost lost.

sousta.name: Sousta
sousta.era: Ancient roots (linked to the Pyrrhic war-dance tradition); name from Venetian 'sousta' (carriage spring)
sousta.tagline: Cretan/Dodecanese couples courtship dance with hopping steps.
sousta.profile: A Greek folk dance performed at weddings as courtship between partners; prominent in Crete, the Dodecanese and the broader Aegean, and described as second only to the syrtos in commonness. A three-step dance with a 'hopping' bounce - two jump-steps forward, one back - with crossed-over linked hands symbolizing unity. Carries symbolism of romance and marriage; historically a socialisation rite among village youth. Music typically on Cretan or Pontian lyra (or violin), laouto, and mandolin/askomandoura. Named from the Venetian word for a carriage spring, reflecting its bouncy motion (English Wikipedia; IJESSR).
sousta.insight: The sousta exists in many officially documented island variants (Crete, Rhodes, Halki, Leros, Kalymnos, Karpathos, Kos, Tilos, Samos, Symi); on Rhodes alone scholars record distinct village forms in a peer-reviewed IJESSR study.

skon.name: Skočná
skon.tagline: rapid Slavic folk-dance, normally in 24 metre
skon.profile: Skočná is a rapid Slavic folk-dance, normally in 24 metre. Czech composers Antonín Dvořák and Bedřich Smetana used this dance, the latter in the third act of The Bartered Bride where it is danced by a circus troupe and is often known as the Dance of the Comedians. Dvořák's 5th, 7th and 11th Slavonic Dances are in the form of the skočná.

syrtos.name: Syrtos
syrtos.tagline: One of the oldest, most widespread Greek chain dances.
syrtos.profile: A collective name for a family of Greek folk dances; open circle/curving line, dancers link hands facing right, led by a leader who improvises and may break away. Among the most ancient Greek dances, described by Lucian (c. AD 125-190). Mainland versions (Peloponnese, Thessaly, Macedonia, Thrace) use 7/8; Crete, the Aegean, Asia Minor and Constantinople use 4/4 (slow-quick-quick). Traditionally segregated lines of men and women, the leader holding the second dancer by a handkerchief; played on regional instruments (Cretan lyra/violin, laouto, clarinet). Central to weddings and religious festivals (English Wikipedia; Britannica).
syrtos.insight: Syrtos and kalamatianos share identical steps but differ in meter (4/4 vs 7/8); the name derives from syro, 'to drag/lead' (English Wikipedia; Britannica).

schuhplattler.name: Schuhplattler
schuhplattler.era: Possible medieval roots; modern regulated form 19th c.
schuhplattler.profile: The Schuhplattler is a folk dance of the Eastern Alps (Upper Bavaria, Tyrol, Salzburg) in which men stomp, clap and strike the soles of their shoes (Schuhe), thighs and knees with flat (platt) hands. It is often a couple dance: men perform leaps and slapping sequences to the Landler portion of the music in 3/4 time (originally zither and guitar, later accordion), while women in dirndls twirl; a boys-only form (reiner Burschenplattler) also exists. The tradition is preserved by Trachtenvereine (costume clubs) in Bavaria, Austria and German-immigrant communities worldwide (English Wikipedia; Society of Folk Dance Historians).
schuhplattler.insight: Often said to mimic the courtship display of the Auerhahn (wood grouse); the modern form was popularized after locals performed it for King Maximilian II of Bavaria on 15 July 1858, and the first Schuhplattler society formed at Miesbach in 1861 (English Wikipedia).

tsifteteli.name: Tsifteteli
tsifteteli.era: Ottoman-era origin; entered the Greek mainland after the 1922 population exchange
tsifteteli.tagline: The Greek 'belly dance' in 4/4, of Anatolian origin.
tsifteteli.profile: A rhythm and dance of Anatolia and the Balkans, the Greek counterpart of Turkish ciftetelli (Turkish 'double-stringed,' from a violin technique). In Greece it functions as the Greek 'belly dance': a solo improvisational form with hip undulations, shoulder shimmies and sinuous arm movements, typically in 4/4 (also cited as 2/4). Performed informally at weddings, glentia and festivals, mostly initiated by women; also professionally in tavernas and bouzouki clubs. Accompanied by violin, bouzouki and percussion; common in rebetiko/laiko (English Wikipedia; Folkdance Footnotes).
tsifteteli.insight: Greek tsifteteli (one 'l') and Turkish ciftetelli (double 'l') share Ottoman roots but are documented as separate Wikipedia/Wikidata entities; Greeks often use 'tsifteteli' as a synonym for oriental dance generally.

tambourin.name: Tambourin
tambourin.tagline: A lively Provençal dance and its namesake tenor drum, defined by a duple meter rhythm.
tambourin.profile: The tambourin is a traditional dance from the Provence region of France, characterized by its lively duple meter and a repetitive, bass-heavy musical structure. The dance takes its name from the tambourin de Provence, a deep, cylindrical tenor drum that is played in tandem with a galoubet, a small three-holed flute. While the instrument has roots dating back to the 11th century, the dance gained significant prominence in 18th-century European art music through the works of composers like Jean-Philippe Rameau. Today, the term refers both to the specific Provençal percussion instrument and the rhythmic, energetic dance style it accompanies.
tambourin.insight: The tambourin dance is named after the instrument that provides its pulse: a deep, two-headed drum played by a single musician who simultaneously operates a three-holed pipe called a galoubet.
sources: Source: Tambourin on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tambourin
tambourin.profile_long:
The tambourin is a dance and musical form deeply rooted in the cultural landscape of Provence, France. Central to its identity is the tambourin de Provence, a deep, two-headed drum of Arabic origin, which has been documented in the region as early as the 1080s. This instrument is distinct for its construction and the method of its performance; a single musician, known as a tambourinaire, plays the drum with a beater in the right hand while simultaneously playing a three-holed flute, the galoubet, with the left. The drum itself is typically suspended from the player's left arm or elbow by a strap, allowing for a unique, integrated performance of melody and rhythm. The dance is named for this instrument, as the music is designed to mimic the drum's repetitive, low-pitched, and resonant character, usually featuring a persistent bass figure that provides a steady, driving pulse. 

During the 18th century, the tambourin transcended its regional Provençal roots to become a popular form in European art music. Composers such as Jean-Philippe Rameau incorporated the dance into various operas, including 'Platée' and 'Les Indes galantes', often utilizing the keyboard to capture the rhythmic vitality of the original folk dance. The dance is characterized by its lively duple meter, which creates a bright, energetic atmosphere. Other notable composers of the era, including Handel and Gluck, also integrated the tambourin into their compositions, cementing its place in the broader classical repertoire. 

Technically, the tambourin de Provence is a sophisticated instrument. It is constructed with a height roughly double its diameter, typically measuring 35 to 40 cm in width and 75 to 80 cm in height. The drum features a 'chanterelle'—a fine gut or hemp string—stretched across the striking head to provide a distinct timbre. The tension of the skins is managed through a system of ropes and leather 'coulants' (sliders), allowing the player to adjust the pitch. The drum is played with a 'massette', a wooden beater designed for precise striking. While the Provençal tambourin is the most iconic, other variants exist, such as the Catalan 'tamborí', which is smaller and often used in the 'cobla' ensembles that accompany the sardana. These regional variations highlight the instrument's versatility and its enduring role in traditional celebrations, parades, and street performances. Despite its historical presence in operas and sonatas, the tambourin remains a living tradition in Provence, where the sound of the pipe and tabor continues to define the rhythmic identity of local festivities.

cabbage-patch.profile: The Cabbage Patch is a hip-hop dance move that involves moving one's clenched fists together in front of the body in a horizontal, circular motion. The hips may be gyrated in sync with these arm movements. The dance became popular in the 1980s, showing up in many dance clubs in North America. The dance's name is derived from the Cabbage Patch Kids dolls or the use of "cabbage" as slang for paper money. The dance was originally celebratory and often associated with being cool.

floss.profile_long:
The Floss, also known as the 'dental floss dance' or 'baile del hilo dental', is a movement-based dance characterized by the rapid, repetitive swinging of arms with clenched fists. The motion involves moving the arms from the back of the body to the front on alternating sides, accompanied by counter-hip movements. The name is derived from the visual impression of the movements, which resemble the act of using a large, invisible piece of dental floss. 

The dance's history is rooted in early internet video culture. While it achieved viral status in 2017, the earliest documented instance of the dance was published on October 18, 2010, by the YouTube channel Ryan Mayall. Another early instance was promoted in a 2014 clip by JStuStudios, featuring content creators Justin Stewart and Andrew Scites, who referred to the move as 'The Squeege'. The dance reached a massive global audience in May 2017, when 14-year-old Russell Horning, known as 'the backpack kid', performed the move during a live Saturday Night Live performance of Katy Perry's song 'Swish Swish'. 

Following this performance, the Floss became a widespread trend among children and teenagers, appearing on numerous children's television channels and in mainstream media such as The Simpsons. Its popularity was further cemented by its inclusion as a limited-time emote in the 2017 video game Fortnite Battle Royale. This integration led to the dance becoming a common sight in schools, though it also sparked controversy. In December 2018, Horning's mother filed a lawsuit against Epic Games for copyright infringement, which resulted in other developers, such as Playground Games, removing similar emotes from their titles to avoid potential litigation. In some educational settings, such as the Ilfracombe Junior School in Devon, England, the dance was banned due to perceived associations with bullying and violence. Despite these controversies, the Floss remains a recognizable cultural artifact of the late 2010s digital era.

formation-dance.profile: Formation dance is a style of ballroom dancing performed by teams of couples arranged in formations. It involves synchronized choreography where couples execute patterns such as diamonds, circles, and lines. Routines last about six minutes and combine individual couple technique with coordinated team movements. Formation dancing is practiced internationally in both Latin and Standard ballroom styles, often in competition.
formation-dance.insight: Formation dancing began in 1932 at London's Astoria Ballroom, evolving into a competitive sport with teams of 6-8 couples performing synchronized routines judged on patterns and synchronicity.
sources: Source: Formation dance on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formation_dance
formation-dance.profile_long: Formation dance originated in 1932 at the Astoria Ballroom in London, introduced by Olive Ripman under the name "pattern dancing." It quickly became a competitive dance form, with contests beginning in England in the 1930s and spreading worldwide. Teams typically consist of 6 to 8 couples who perform choreographed routines that combine individual dancesport techniques with coordinated group patterns. These patterns, also called shapes or images, include diamonds, squares, diagonals, circles, and lines, and the clarity and transitions of these shapes are key judging criteria. The choreography may be based on a single dance or a medley of dances, with Latin formation including Cha Cha, Rumba, Jive, Paso Doble, and Samba, and Standard formation including Waltz, Quickstep, Tango, Viennese Waltz, and Foxtrot. Routines last up to six minutes, including walk-on and walk-off sections often featuring free-form choreography and lifts, which are prohibited during the judged segment. Synchronization and timing to the music's beat are critical, with judges marking teams on synchronicity and execution. Formation dance is governed internationally by the International DanceSport Federation (IDSF), with competitions such as the British National Championships at the Blackpool Dance Festival and the Donaupokal Invitational in Vienna. In German-speaking countries, formation teams follow similar rules under the Deutscher Tanzsportverband (DTV) and World DanceSport Federation (WDSF), with music structured into an entrance, main part, and exit, separated by gong signals. Music themes vary widely, often arranged from known pieces to suit the dance character. Special figures unique to formation dancing include roundabouts, chain reactions, and the Velberter Rose, which add visual impact. Men's attire in Standard formation is traditionally black or midnight blue tailcoats, while Latin formation allows more color but requires uniformity. Formation dancing remains a living tradition with active international competition and evolving choreography.

liscio.name: Liscio
liscio.tagline: Northern Italy, 19th century — the smooth ballroom dance of Romagna and Emilia, where the Viennese waltz, mazurka, polka, and schottische we
liscio.profile: Liscio or ballo liscio ("smooth" or "smooth dance" respectively in Italian) is a genre of music originating in the 19th century in the northern Italian region of Romagna under the influence of Viennese ballroom dances including the mazurka, waltz, polka, schottische, march. It later became popular and spread to the rest of the country. The accordion, which was also a 19th-century invention, features prominently. The tradition contrasts with older Italian folk dances in which the fiddle was the primary instrument.
liscio.insight: Raoul Casadei — bandleader of Italy's most famous liscio orchestra across six decades — produced over a thousand songs and turned ballo liscio into a national pop genre during the 1970s and 80s; his 1973 'Ciao Mare' remains the unofficial anthem of the Italian Adriatic coast, played at every sagra (village festival) from Ravenna to Rimini.

one-step.tagline: Turkey, 20th century — The One-Step was a ballroom dance popular in social dancing at the beginning of the 20th century
one-step.profile: The One-Step was a ballroom dance popular in social dancing at the beginning of the 20th century. Troy Kinney writes that One-Step originated from the Turkey Trot dance, with all mannerisms of the latter removed, so that "of the original 'trot' nothing remains but the basic step". The One-Step included the following basic figures (and a number of more advanced ones): The Castle Walk (invented and introduced by Mr. and Mrs. Vernon Castle). The Turn is a walking step, pivoting on one foot to change direction.
one-step.insight: (1) From posterior third position, the right foot steps to  anterior fourth position; (2) left foot glides to  second position; (3) right foot glides into first position; (4) left foot steps back to posterior fourth position; (5) right foot steps to anterior third position.

new-vogue.name: New Vogue
new-vogue.tagline: An Australian form of ballroom sequence dancing originating in the 1930s
new-vogue.profile: The New Vogue dance style is an Australian form of ballroom sequence dancing that originated in the 1930s. It has since become an important part in the Australian and New Zealand ballroom scene and is one of the three Dancesport styles in Australia, alongside traditional Ballroom and Latin American. All New Vogue dances are based on a sequence of dance steps which are continually repeated, usually until the music ends. These sequences are always either 16 or 32 bars long, and require music that is in turn sequenced.
new-vogue.insight: Originating in 1930s Australia, New Vogue sequence dances always run for exactly 16 or 32 bars, making them uniquely approachable for beginners.
sources: Source: New Vogue on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Vogue
new-vogue.profile_long: The New Vogue dance style is an Australian form of ballroom sequence dancing that originated in the 1930s. It has since become an important part in the Australian and New Zealand ballroom scene and is one of the three Dancesport styles in Australia, alongside traditional Ballroom and Latin American. All New Vogue dances are based on a sequence of dance steps which are continually repeated, usually until the music ends. These sequences are always either 16 or 32 bars long, and require music that is in turn sequenced. Due to the nature of the dances they are much easier to pick up by beginners than Latin dances, and as such, beginner dancers are less likely to feel overwhelmed when learning them and can perform the dances to a respectable level within a short time of learning. New Vogue dances can be danced at different levels, with higher levels requiring more precise steps and the addition of arm and torso movement, known as styling. This makes the dances easy to pick up but hard to master. New Vogue Dances are based on one of several sub categories, including Viennese Waltz Rhythm, Slow Foxtrot Rhythm, March Rhythm and Tango Rhythm. Out of the many New Vogue Dances, fifteen are recognised by Dancesport Australia for use in DanceSport competitions. These competition dances include the Barclay Blues, Carousel, Charmaine, Evening Three Step, Excelsior Schottische, Gypsy Tap, La Bomba, Lucille Waltz, Merrilyn, Parma Waltz, Swing Waltz, Tangoette, Tango Terrific, Tracie Leigh Waltz, and Twilight Waltz. These dances vary in length and difficulty, and the harder dances are performed at higher levels. The New Vogue Dances are competed in all DanceSport divisions, including recreational, amateur, professional, ability dance/special dance, vision impaired dance, and para dance. Since 2019, the Services Club in Canowindra, NSW, has hosted a 12-hour event in late June featuring only Australian New Vogue Dances to live music, attracting participants from all over Australia. Further technical details of the championship and competition dances have been documented by authors such as Neville Boyd and Russ Hesketh.

samba-funk.name: Samba funk
samba-funk.profile: Samba funk is primarily a musical subgenre fusing samba with American funk, originating in the late 1960s with pianist Dom Salvador and Grupo Abolicao (precursor to Banda Black Rio). A related ballroom dance offshoot, 'samba-funkeado,' was created by dance teacher Jimmy de Oliveira, mixing samba de gafieira with funk. It is frequently conflated with samba-rock/samba-soul.

swing.name: Swing
swing.tagline: A family of social dances originating in 1920s–1940s United States jazz culture.
swing.profile: Swing is a diverse family of social dances that evolved alongside jazz music in the United States during the 1920s and 1930s. Primarily rooted in African-American vernacular traditions, these dances are characterized by rhythmic improvisation, a signature 'bounce,' and a variety of partner connections. While the term 'swing' was initially applied to the music, it later became a catch-all for dances like Lindy Hop, Balboa, and Shag. Today, these traditions remain active worldwide through social clubs, competitions, and global workshops.
swing.insight: Lindy Hop, the 'grandfather' of swing dances, emerged in 1927 at Harlem's Savoy Ballroom, where dancers fused jazz rhythms into an energetic, improvisational style that defined the era.

swing.profile_long: Swing dance is a category of social dances that developed with the swing style of jazz music in the 1920s–1940s. The origins of these dances predate the swing era, with the majority beginning in African-American communities as vernacular dances. The Savoy Ballroom in Harlem, New York, served as a fundamental site for the popularization of these styles, particularly the Lindy Hop, which is often cited as the 'grandfather' of swing dances. Historically, the term 'swing' referred to the jazz music itself, which inspired the evolution of the dance, while the term 'jitterbug' was later used to describe the dancers and the dances themselves. The movement is defined by a high degree of physical vigor, improvisation, and a characteristic 'bounce'—a rhythmic compression into the floor that mirrors the ternary rhythm of swing music. As the music evolved from big bands to rhythm and blues and rock 'n' roll, the dances adapted, leading to a wide spectrum of styles including Balboa, Collegiate Shag, and the later West Coast Swing. During the 1940s, the dance spread globally, particularly through the influence of American troops during World War II. While the popularity of big bands waned in the 1970s, a revival beginning in the 1980s and 1990s has seen these dances flourish in social and competitive circuits worldwide. Today, swing dance is practiced in various formats, from social dance halls to structured competitions, and continues to influence modern dance forms.

lyrical-ballet.profile: Lyrical ballet is an offshoot of the now-obsolete Russian lyrical (Soviet ballroom) dances. It is a lilting style of dance that uses the ballet technique along with the Soviet ballroom dance forms. The word lyrical refers to a lilting, poetic feel associated with the movements and the steps flow from the one to the next. It belongs to the genre of classical folk dance.

viennese-waltz.name: Viennese waltz
viennese-waltz.profile: Viennese waltz (German: Wiener Walzer) is a form of ballroom dance. At least four different meanings are recognized. In the historically first sense, the name may refer to several versions of the waltz, including the earliest waltzes done in ballroom dancing, danced to the music of Viennese waltz. What is now called the Viennese waltz is the original form of the waltz. It was the first ballroom dance performed in the closed hold or "waltz" position.

albanian-war-dances.name: Albanian war dances
albanian-war-dances.tagline: Martial sword-and-fire dances re-enacting battle before Albanian warriors fought.
albanian-war-dances.profile: Albanian war dances (Albanian: valle luftarake) were historically performed before departure for battle and now appear at feasts and festivals, differing by region. Early-19th-century Western travellers described a circle dance around a ritual purifying fire, beginning with a battle cry and war drums; the northern-highland sword-dance type spread to the Lezha lowlands via mountain shepherds. The Rugova variant is a mock duel between two men competing for a maiden (English Wikipedia, 'Albanian war dances').
albanian-war-dances.insight: A living relic of pantomimic combat rites linking modern Albanian identity to ancient Illyrian/Pyrrhic martial traditions; the folktale 'Skanderbeg and Ballaban' narrates the sword dance performed by Skanderbeg's soldiers before battle (Robert Elsie, Albanian Folktales and Legends, via English Wikipedia).

adana.name: Adana
adana.tagline: A traditional Macedonian men's folk dance originating from the town of Veles.
adana.profile: Adana is a traditional Macedonian Oro originating from the town of Veles, characterized as a men's dance with a medium-fast tempo. The performance evolves from a controlled, balanced opening in a half-circle formation to a high-energy sequence involving jumps, kneeling, and turns. Dancers initially hold shoulders, transitioning to holding hands as the rhythm accelerates. The dance is structured in a 2/4 meter, reflecting the rhythmic traditions of North Macedonia.
adana.insight: Originating in Veles, North Macedonia, the Adana dance transitions from shoulder-held balancing in a half-circle to a faster, hand-held sequence featuring jumps, kneeling, and turns.
sources: Source: Adana (dance) on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adana_(dance)

video_stack.title: Zoran Dzorlev - DMBUC: oro Adana

adana.profile_long: Adana is a traditional Macedonian Oro, a form of folk dance deeply rooted in the cultural landscape of the town of Veles. As a men's dance, it is defined by a specific progression of intensity and physical engagement. The performance begins with a controlled, balanced movement, performed while the dancers are arranged in a half-circle formation. During this initial phase, the dancers maintain a connection by holding each other's shoulders, a posture that suggests a collective, unified movement. As the dance progresses and the tempo increases, the physical demands shift significantly. The dancers transition from the shoulder-hold to holding hands, allowing for more dynamic movement. This faster phase of the dance incorporates more athletic elements, including jumping, kneeling, and turning. The rhythmic structure of the dance is set to a 2/4 meter. The transition from the initial balancing phase to the more vigorous, faster phase marks the primary structure of the performance. The dance is categorized as a type of Macedonian Oro, a family of dances that typically involve circular or semi-circular formations. The specific movements—balancing, jumping, kneeling, and turning—require a degree of physical coordination and stamina, particularly as the tempo accelerates. Because the dance is described as a 'man dance', it is traditionally performed by men, though the sources do not specify if this is a strict gender restriction or a cultural convention. The dance's origins in Veles connect it to the broader tradition of Macedonian folk dance, which is characterized by its rhythmic complexity and communal nature. The progression from a static, balanced start to an active, high-energy finish is a hallmark of the Adana, reflecting a narrative of building intensity within the performance. The use of the half-circle formation at the start provides a clear spatial orientation for the dancers, which then evolves as the dance accelerates. The transition from shoulder-holding to hand-holding is a key indicator of the change in the dance's energy and the nature of the connection between the participants. The dance remains a documented part of the Macedonian folk tradition, with its specific movements and structure preserved through the cultural practices of the Veles region.

choreia.profile: Choreia (Ancient Greek: χορεία, romanized: choreía) is a circle dance accompanied by singing (see Greek chorus, choros), in ancient Greece. Homer refers to this dance in his epic poem, the Iliad. Terms descended from Greek choreia that are used for circle dances in a number of other countries are: horon, in Turkey khorovod (хоровод), in Russia khora (хора), in Ukraine hora, in Romania and Moldova horo (хоро), in Bulgaria oro (оро), in North Macedonia and Montenegro
choreia.insight: Choreia (Ancient Greek: χορεία, romanized: choreía) is a circle dance accompanied by singing (see Greek chorus, choros), in ancient Greece.

carol.profile: A carol is a festive song, generally religious but not necessarily connected with Christian church worship, and sometimes accompanied by a dance. A caroller (or caroler) is someone who sings carols, and is said to be carolling (or caroling). Today the carol is represented almost exclusively by the Advent carol, the Christmas carol, and to a lesser extent by the Easter carol; however, despite their present association with religion, this has not always been the case.

domkach.name: Domkach
domkach.tagline: Nagpuri wedding dance of joy and satire
domkach.profile: Domkach (or Damkach) is a folk dance of Bihar, Jharkhand and Nepal's Madhesh province, performed during wedding ceremonies; in Bihar it features in the Mithila and Bhojpur regions and in Jharkhand it is a Nagpuri folk dance (Wikipedia). The women and men of the bride's and groom's families form a semicircle holding each other's waists and dance to satirical, joyful songs accompanied by dholak and ghungroo (Wikipedia). In its classic Chotanagpur form, the women of the groom's family perform it through the night after the baraat (wedding procession) has departed, keeping themselves awake and entertained (EZCC).
domkach.insight: The dance is named after the Dambru/Dom musical instrument; Nagpuri Domkach is sub-classified into Ekharia, Dohri and Jhumta variants, and the wedding-season run extends from Deouthan in Kartik (Oct-Nov) to the Rath Yatra in Ashadh (Jun-Jul) (Wikipedia).

daychovo-horo.name: Daychovo horo
daychovo-horo.era: Originated in North Bulgaria; popularized post-WWII
daychovo-horo.tagline: Northern Bulgarian 9/8 circle dance with a calling leader.
daychovo-horo.profile: A Bulgarian folk dance in nine-beat meter (9/16 or 9/8), the Daychovo-type rhythm being 2+2+2+3. Unusual in being a circle dance that nevertheless has a leader who calls figures/variations. Traditionally danced 'na prava' (straight line) by men grasping neighbors' belts in an X, or in an open mixed circle with V handhold. Originating in North Bulgaria, accompanied by gaida, gadulka, kaval, accordion and tapan (English Wikipedia; Folk Dance Federation of California).
daychovo-horo.insight: The name means 'Daycho's dance.' Per dance researcher Boris Conev (via Dick Crum), it traces to a 19th-century Pleven cattle merchant named Daycho whose downfall after 1878 inspired derisive tavern lyrics set to a lively 9/16 melody (Folk Dance Federation of California).

conga-line.name: Conga line
conga-line.tagline: Carnival processional line dance from Cuba.
conga-line.profile: The conga line is a novelty line dance derived from the Cuban carnival conga (comparsa) of Santiago de Cuba, where neighborhood comparsas march in serpentine processions (arrollando) descended from Afro-Cuban Congolese cabildos. Dancers form a line, each holding the waist of the person ahead, with three shuffle steps and a kick on the fourth beat, to a staccato conga-drum rhythm (plus the corneta china in Santiago). It became a US craze in the 1930s-1950s, popularized by Desi Arnaz and Xavier Cugat (English Wikipedia; Harvard ReVista).
conga-line.insight: The conga was one of the earliest successful 20th-century Cuban musical exports, helping prepare international audiences for son, mambo and salsa - even as it was banned at times in Cuba as a dangerous mass gathering (English Wikipedia; Harvard ReVista).

corridinho.name: Corridinho
corridinho.tagline: Portugal — form of Portuguese folk dance, namely in the Algarve region
corridinho.profile: The corridinho is a form of Portuguese folk dance, namely in the Algarve region. The origin of the dance itself is unclear and believed older, although it gained popularity in the 1800s. The name derives from correr, to run which partly describes this type of dance. The dance was performed in a round (dança de roda) in the open air. The oldest musical instruments recorded were small flutes or fifes (pífaro) and harmonicas, (harmónica) until the accordion was implemented and dominated ever since.
corridinho.insight: The corridinho is a form of Portuguese folk dance, namely in the Algarve region.

dances-of-universal-peace.name: Dances of Universal Peace
dances-of-universal-peace.tagline: United States — spiritual practice that employs singing and dancing the sacred phrases of the world's religions
dances-of-universal-peace.profile: The Dances of Universal Peace (DUP) are a spiritual practice that employs singing and dancing the sacred phrases of the world's religions. Their intention is to raise consciousness and promote peace between diverse religions according to one stated goal. The DUP are of North American Sufic origin. They combine chants from many world faiths with dancing, whirling, and a variety of movement with singing.
dances-of-universal-peace.insight: The very first dance took place on 16 March, 1968 in San Francisco, California.

assyrian-folk-dance.name: Assyrian folk dance
assyrian-folk-dance.tagline: Assyrian folk dances are sets of dances that are performed throughout the world by Assyrians, mostly on occ…
assyrian-folk-dance.profile: Assyrian folk dances are sets of dances that are performed throughout the world by Assyrians, mostly on occasions such as weddings, community parties and other jubilant events. Assyrian folk dances are mainly made up of circle dances like ballet that are performed in a line, which may be straight, curved, or both. Most of the dances allow unlimited number of participants, with the exception of the Sabre Dance, which require three at most. Assyrian dances would vary from weak to strong, depending on the mood and tempo of a song.
assyrian-folk-dance.insight:
== History ==

Lily Oraham Taimoorazy, sometimes considered to be the mother of Assyrian folk dancing, founded a dance group called the Shamiram Folkloric Group in Tehran in 1957.

cachua.profile: The cachua (qachwa, qhaswa, kashua, kaswa, kachura) (ˈqɑt͡ʃwa or ˈχɑt͡ʃwa, diminutive form cachuita) is a Latin-American baroque dance form found mainly in Peru. It still exists today as a circle dance. The term comes from the Quechua language qhachwa, meaning "round dance", via Spanish. It was also applied to some villancicos to Spanish texts with cachua rhythm, such as two examples in a report submitted to Charles IV of Spain c.1788-1790. It is in rapid unsyncopated 2/4 time.

faroese-chain-dance.name: Faroese chain dance
faroese-chain-dance.tagline: The national circle dance of the Faroe Islands, danced to traditional ballads called kvæði.
faroese-chain-dance.profile: The Faroese chain dance is a medieval circle dance from the Faroe Islands, performed holding hands in a continuous chain. It is accompanied solely by singing of kvæði, traditional Faroese ballads, without instruments. Dancers move slowly leftward with a characteristic six-step pattern, expressing the ballads' narrative through gestures and facial expressions.
faroese-chain-dance.insight: At Ólavsøka, the Faroe Islands' national holiday, dancers form unbroken circles that swell and contract, passing face-to-face twice each round.
sources: Source: Faroese chain dance on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faroese_chain_dance
faroese-chain-dance.profile_long: The Faroese chain dance (Faroese: Føroyskur dansur) is the national folk dance of the Faroe Islands, rooted in medieval tradition and preserved as a living cultural practice. It is performed in a circle or chain formation where dancers hold hands—right hand overlapping the left of the neighbor—and move rhythmically to the left with a distinctive six-step pattern called stígingarstev. The dance is accompanied exclusively by the singing of kvæði, Faroese ballads that narrate heroic or historical stories. The lead singer, called the skipari, must know all verses, while the rest join in at the chorus. The dancers' movements and expressions reflect the ballad's emotions, such as clenching hands during battle scenes or cheering at moments of victory. When many dancers join, the circle bends inward, forming multiple concentric chains, with dancers passing face-to-face twice per round. Variations include the trokingarstev, where dancers stand mostly still or move backward during verses and step forward during refrains, favored in southern islands like Suðuroy, and the bandadansur or ribbon dance, where men and women stand in two rows holding ribbons, raising them during refrains to form tunnels through which dancers pass. The dance is traditionally practiced during the dark winter months, from autumn until Lent, with many Faroese dance associations active today, including some in Denmark. The dance is performed without instrumental music, relying solely on vocal ballads and rhythmic foot stamping. It remains a vibrant tradition, showcased notably at the national holiday Ólavsøka, where large groups dance late into the night. The Faroese chain dance is a rare example of a medieval circle dance still practiced in its original form, emphasizing communal singing and movement without instrumental accompaniment.

ganggangsullae.name: Ganggangsullae
ganggangsullae.tagline: Korean women's moonlit harvest circle dance
ganggangsullae.profile: Ganggangsullae is a seasonal harvest and fertility ritual of southwestern Korea, performed primarily at Chuseok (Korean Thanksgiving) in the eighth lunar month (UNESCO). Under the full moon, women join hands in a circle and sing and dance all night under a lead singer, with the group answering the refrain 'ganggangsullae'; during interludes they mime farm and fishing-village vignettes. Traditionally performed only by women at night without instruments, it offered a rare freedom from restrictive Joseon-era rules governing rural young women.
ganggangsullae.insight: Designated an Important Intangible Cultural Property of Korea in 1966 and inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List in 2009, ganggangsullae is now taught in elementary-school music curricula and performed nationwide as a representative Korean folk art (UNESCO; Korea Heritage Service).

janani-jhumar.name: Janani Jhumar
janani-jhumar.tagline: A women-centric folk dance of the Chota Nagpur Plateau, Jharkhand
janani-jhumar.profile: Janani Jhumar is a women-centric folk dance originating from the Chota Nagpur Plateau region of Jharkhand. Characterized by its feminine grace, the dance involves participants holding hands in a linear formation that moves in a circular path. While women lead the singing and movement, men provide the rhythmic accompaniment using traditional instruments like the mandar, dhol, and bansi. The dance is deeply tied to the agricultural and ritual calendar, performed during the festivals of Karam and Jitiya.
janani-jhumar.insight: In the Chota Nagpur Plateau, Janani Jhumar begins with the monsoon rains in Ashadh and continues until the Kartik festival, marking the transition from agricultural labor to the marriage season.
sources: Source: Janani Jhumar on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Janani_Jhumar
janani-jhumar.profile_long:
Janani Jhumar, also known as Janani Jhumair, is a traditional folk dance form native to the Chota Nagpur Plateau in the Indian state of Jharkhand. It is a distinctly women-centric performance, serving as a vital expression of the community's cultural and seasonal life. The dance is performed during specific times of the year, beginning in the month of Ashadh, which corresponds to June and July, and continuing through the month of Kartik, which falls in October and November. This period aligns with the agricultural cycle and the celebration of significant festivals such as Karam and Jitiya. When the dance is performed within the domestic space of a courtyard, it is referred to as Angnai.

The performance structure of Janani Jhumar is defined by its circular movement. Women participants hold each other's hands, forming a linear line that progresses in a circle. The aesthetic of the dance is described as having feminine grace, reflecting the cultural identity of the women who perform it. While the women are the primary dancers and singers, the musical foundation is provided by men who play traditional instruments. The ensemble typically includes the mandar, a double-headed drum; the dhol, another variety of drum; and the bansi, a flute. This collaborative effort between the dancers and the musicians creates a rhythmic environment that sustains the performance throughout the festivals.

Janani Jhumar is highly diverse, with numerous variants categorized by both occasion and regional influence. The courtyard version, Angnai, is further subdivided into types such as Chandhantari, Pahilsanjha, Adhratiya, Bhinsariya, Udhaowa, Thadauwa, Lahasua, Khemta, Daiddhara, and Raskrida. These variations reflect the specific timing or thematic focus of the performance. Additionally, regional styles are classified based on their geographical origin, including Purbaha, Pachhimaha, Uttaraha, Dakshinaha, Sonpuriya, Nagpuriya, Jashpuriya, Gangpuriya, Henthghatiya, and Assamiya. These classifications highlight the widespread practice and regional adaptation of the dance across the Chota Nagpur Plateau.

The dance season concludes as the marriage season approaches, at which point the community transitions to other traditional forms such as the Domkach dance. This cyclical nature of performance underscores the role of Janani Jhumar as a marker of time and social transition within the region. As a living tradition, it remains a central component of the cultural heritage of the Chota Nagpur Plateau, maintained through the active participation of the community during the designated months of the year.

jhumair.name: Jhumair
jhumair.era: Traditional; agrarian roots in the Chota Nagpur plateau
jhumair.tagline: Sadan harvest dance of the Chota Nagpur plateau
jhumair.profile: Jhumair (Jhumar) is a folk dance of the Sadan - the Indo-Aryan ethnic groups of Chotanagpur - performed across Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Bihar, Assam and West Bengal, and also by Adivasi communities, mainly associated with the harvest season (Wikipedia). Performers stand in a row or circle, hold hands, sing couplets, sway, clap and perform timed jumps, accompanied by the mandar, dhol, nagara and bansuri. Regional and stylistic varieties include Nagpuri, Khortha, Kurmali and Panchpargania Jhumar, plus the gendered Mardani (men's) and Janani (women's) Jhumar (Wikipedia; Historified).
jhumair.insight: Folk artist Mukund Nayak of Jharkhand is a celebrated exponent of Nagpuri Jhumar, having taught and recorded the form for decades to preserve its Sadan roots (Grokipedia, citing Ranchi University records).

ghost-dance.name: Ghost Dance
ghost-dance.tagline: Native American religious circle dance of renewal — NOT Chinese
ghost-dance.profile: The Ghost Dance (Caddo: Nanissáanah, also 'Ghost Dance of 1890') is a ceremony and new religious movement of Native American peoples, founded on the millenarian teachings of the Northern Paiute prophet Wovoka (Jack Wilson) in 1889 (English Wikipedia; Britannica). Based on the traditional round/circle dance, it spread across the Western United States and is associated with the 1890 Wounded Knee Massacre. There is no genuine Chinese dance by this name.
ghost-dance.insight: A profoundly significant Indigenous North American spiritual movement of cultural revitalization and resistance; it must be treated respectfully as a sacred ceremony, not entertainment (Britannica; World History Encyclopedia).

kalamatianos.name: Kalamatianos
kalamatianos.era: Roots in antiquity; modern name from the town of Kalamata
kalamatianos.profile: One of Greece's best-known dances, widely regarded as the national dance; danced in a chain/open circle, counterclockwise, dancers holding hands. Beat 7/8 subdivided 3+2+2 (slow-quick-quick); 12 steps over 4 bars (10 forward counterclockwise, 2 back). The lead dancer often holds the second by a handkerchief to perform elaborate steps and acrobatics. Inclusive (men, women, children); performed at weddings, festivals and diaspora gatherings, accompanied by clarinet, violin, laouto, drums and often bouzouki (English Wikipedia; Costa Navarino).
kalamatianos.insight: Steps are identical to the syrtos but the meter differs (kalamatianos 7/8, syrtos 4/4); the kalamatianos is on Greece's National Inventory of Intangible Cultural Heritage (a national, not UNESCO, recognition).

halay.name: Halay
halay.tagline: Turkey's signature line dance — hands joined, davul and zurna driving the village floor.
halay.profile: Halay is the national dance of Turkey. It refers to all traditional circular and line dances performed across the country. The term is used among Turks, Kurds, Arabs, and Asia Minor Greeks (particularly Pontic Greeks, Karamanlides, and Cappadocian Greeks). Circular and line dances in Turkey are commonly performed at weddings and festive gatherings, traditionally accompanied by the zurna and davul, or sometimes by the singing of the dancers themselves. In recent years, electronic instruments have increasingly been used in place of traditional musical instruments.
halay.insight: The earliest known written definition of the word halay appears in the 1932 ethnographic compilation Anadilden Derlemeler by Hamit Zübeyir Koşay and İshak Işıtman, where halay is defined as a hand-held line dance from Central Anatolia, accompanied by the zurna and davul.

garba.name: Garba
garba.tagline: Gujarati devotional circle dance of Navaratri
garba.profile: Garba is a ritualistic and devotional folk dance of Gujarat performed during the Hindu festival of Navaratri, dedicated to the worship of feminine energy (Shakti) (UNESCO). Dancers move counter-clockwise in a circle around a perforated earthenware pot lit with a lamp (garbo) or an image of the mother goddess Amba, using simple steps, singing and clapping that build from slow circular movements to fast whirling (UNESCO). The name derives from a Sanskrit word for womb, implying life and creation, and the dance fosters social and gender inclusivity across communities.
garba.insight: Garba was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity on 6 December 2023 at the 18th session in Kasane, Botswana, becoming India's 15th element on the list (UNESCO/PIB).

mardani-jhumar.name: Mardani Jhumar
mardani-jhumar.tagline: The martial men's variant of the Jhumair harvest dance
mardani-jhumar.profile: Mardani Jhumar (also Mardana Jhumair) is the vigorous, martial men's variant of the Jhumar/Jhumair folk dance of the Sadan (Nagpuri-speaking, Indo-Aryan) and Adivasi communities of the Chotanagpur region, performed in Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Odisha (Wikipedia, Jhumair; Folk dances of Jharkhand). Danced by men after the harvest at fairs, performers wear ghungroo and dance in a circle holding each other's hands, with movements reflecting masculine and martial energy (the Veera/valorous mood); some sources class it, like the Paika, as a semi-martial form (EZCC). Musical accompaniment includes the mandar, nagara, dhak and shehnai/bansi (EZCC; Wikipedia).
mardani-jhumar.insight: Mardani Jhumar is the male counterpart to Janani Jhumar (the women's variant); together they form part of the Nagpuri dance-song repertoire, distinguishing it from the parent Jhumair tradition while remaining closely related to it (Wikipedia, Jhumair).

kantu.name: Kantu
kantu.tagline: Peru — n ancient style of music and circle dance which is widespread since incaic or even preincaic epoch on the P…
kantu.profile: Kantu or k'antu is an ancient style of music and circle dance which is widespread since incaic or even preincaic epoch on the Peruvian and Bolivian highlands. Modern versions of this style still use the Quechua or Aymara language and the siku (ceremonial panpipe). Some musicologists argue that the name for this style comes from the Spanish word 'canto' meaning 'song.' Linguists might argue that the name comes from the Quechua word 'k'antu' which is a widely known flower in Bolivia. Also, k'antu may be a word of extinct Puquina language with unknown meaning.
kantu.insight: Kantu or k'antu is an ancient style of music and circle dance which is widespread since incaic or even preincaic epoch on the Peruvian and Bolivian highlands.

khigga.name: Khigga
khigga.tagline: style of Assyrian folk dance in which multiple dancers hold each other's hands and form a semi-circle or a …
khigga.profile: Khigga is a style of Assyrian folk dance in which multiple dancers hold each other's hands and form a semi-circle or a curved line. There are multiple foot patterns that dancers perform. Its thought to have been danced for thousands of years. It is one of the most common and simplest Assyrian folk dances, generally performed at weddings, baptisms, confirmations and other joyous occasions. Set in common time, khigga is accompanied by a moderate dance beat and is usually performed to Assyrian folk and pop music.
khigga.insight: This Syrian khigga form is generally danced from left to right and it also is the first beat danced in a Syrian-Assyrian wedding when the married couple are welcomed in the reception.

manau.name: Manau
manau.tagline: India — traditional ceremony common to the Kachin (or Jinghpaw) people of northern Myanmar (Burma), Yunnan, China a…
manau.profile: The manau (Burmese: မနော; Chinese: 目瑙纵歌; pinyin: Mùnǎo zònggē) dance is a traditional ceremony common to the Kachin (or Jinghpaw) people of northern Myanmar (Burma), Yunnan, China and Arunachal Pradesh, India. Although the majority of Kachin people are Christian, the manau has its roots in animistic religion. The manau ground where the ceremony takes place is the cultural center of Kachin communities. Manaus can be held throughout the year, but the biggest manau dance, the sut manau, is held in January.
manau.insight: Many Kachin towns hold manau dances, with the largest celebrations taking place in Myitkyina, the capital of Kachin State in Myanmar, in Laiza, the capital of the Kachin Independence Organization (KIO), and in Ruili, a center of Kachin culture in Yunnan, China.

malho.name: Malhao
malho.tagline: Lively Portuguese folk couples dance from the Minho.
malho.profile: Malhao is a lively Portuguese folk dance and song from northwestern Portugal, especially the Minho region, danced by couples in lines or circular formation with quick rhythmic footwork, accompanied by guitarra portuguesa and tambourine. Its name likely derives from an agricultural implement; the song tells of the 'malhao' (winnower), reflecting rural harvest-celebration origins. Performed at festivals such as Festa das Cruzes in Barcelos (Portugal.com; Society of Folk Dance Historians).
malho.insight: Malhao has many local variants ('Malhao de Cinfaes,' 'Malhao de Agueda') recorded by fado singer Amalia Rodrigues; per folk-dance historians it has changed little in over a century.

rom-kbach.name: Rom kbach
rom-kbach.tagline: Thailand — genre of Cambodian popular music and a popular Khmer dance style
rom-kbach.profile: Rom kbach (Khmer: រាំក្បាច់) is a genre of Cambodian popular music and a popular Khmer dance style. Rom kbach has a slower emotional melody similar to Thai music, whereas the Chamrieng Samai music category of romvong has a faster tune. The two main cultural dance styles of Cambodia are the romvong and rom kbach, however the lam leav and saravan dance styles are also popular. They have their roots in ancient cultural traditions.
rom-kbach.insight: Rom kbach (Khmer: រាំក្បាច់) is a genre of Cambodian popular music and a popular Khmer dance style.

roda.name: Roda
roda.tagline: Ambiguous 'circle'; best-supported referent is Samba de Roda.
roda.profile: 'Roda' means circle/wheel and is ambiguous: it can denote the capoeira roda or, most defensibly as a dance, Samba de Roda of the Reconcavo of Bahia - a music-dance-poetry tradition from 17th-century Bahia drawing on enslaved Africans' traditions plus Portuguese elements. Performers form a circle (roda); a soloist dances in the center using the umbigada (belly-bump) to invite a successor, with footwork, leg and hip movements, accompanied by atabaque, berimbau, pandeiro, chocalho, singing and clapping (UNESCO; English Wikipedia).
roda.insight: Samba de Roda was proclaimed a UNESCO Masterpiece in 2005 and inscribed on the Representative List in 2008 (file 00101); it influenced the urban samba that became a Brazilian national symbol (UNESCO).

mayim-mayim.name: Mayim Mayim
mayim-mayim.tagline: Circle dance of joy at finding water in the desert
mayim-mayim.profile: Mayim Mayim ('water, water') is an Israeli folk circle dance. Per Wikipedia, the dance was created in 1937 for a festival to celebrate the discovery of water in Kibbutz Naan after a seven-year search; the choreographer was Else I. Dublon. The music was composed by Emanuel Amiran (Pugashov) and the lyrics taken from Isaiah 12:3 ('Joyfully shall you draw water from the wells of salvation') (Wikipedia, Mayim Mayim). It is danced in a circle facing center, hands held except when clapping; its first four counts - the 'Mayim step' - are a grapevine/cherkessia step that became known to Israelis through this dance.
mayim-mayim.insight: Mayim Mayim has spread far beyond Israel - it became a fixture of Japanese school physical-education classes after being introduced during the post-war American occupation - and is often performed at international folk dance events (Wikipedia; Unseen Japan).

tamzara.name: Tamzara
tamzara.tagline: Greece — n Armenian folk dance native to the Armenian Highlands
tamzara.profile: Tamzara is an Armenian folk dance native to the Armenian Highlands. In Armenia the dance originally had a ritual character, it was a wedding song and dance. Now "Tamzara" has lost its former ritual significance, when it was performed during almost all community events and parties. It is today performed by Armenians, Assyrians, Azerbaijanis (in the regions of Sharur, Nakhchivan and parts of Iranian Azerbaijan), Greeks and Turks. In post-Soviet Armenia, tamzara dance is gaining more and more popularity among all strata of the population.
tamzara.insight: In 2018, Azerbaijani-style Tamzara, along with kochari, was inscribed into the UNESCO List of Intangible Cultural Heritage with the Yalli dance in need of urgent safeguarding.

ring-shout.name: Ring shout
ring-shout.tagline: America’s deepest sacred dance — counterclockwise circle worship, born in plantation ‘praise houses,’ still danced in coastal Georgia today.
ring-shout.profile: The ring shout is a distinctive African American ritual dance originating with enslaved Africans in the southern United States where worshippers move in a counterclockwise circle while hand-clapping, foot-patting and shuffling, stick-beating to foreground the rhythm, and call-and-response singing. It is an oral tradition passed down in African American families since the era of slavery. Elders and religious leaders pass down songs and shouts to the younger generation.
ring-shout.insight: Musicologist and educator Eileen Southern traced the earliest observance of the ring shout to a 1819 observance of the secret African ritual dances that took place later in the Black quarters of Philadelphia after a Christian camp meeting. Helena Island in South Carolina from 1862 to 1863 and documented several ring shout experiences in praise houses.

pembe.name: Pembe
pembe.tagline: A Macedonian circle dance (oro) from the Veles region featuring a gradual tempo increase.
pembe.profile: Pembe is a traditional Macedonian circle dance originating from the Veles region. It is a mixed-gender dance performed in a half-circle formation with participants holding hands at shoulder height. The movement is defined by steady steps on the whole foot, punctuated by a characteristic heel motion. The dance is structured to begin at a slow tempo, gradually accelerating toward its conclusion.
pembe.insight: Pembe is a Macedonian oro from Veles that transitions from a slow, steady pace to a faster tempo, characterized by distinct heel movements performed while dancers hold hands at shoulder level.

pembe.profile_long: Pembe is a traditional Macedonian circle dance, known as an oro, which originates from the Veles region of North Macedonia. As a cultural expression, it belongs to the broader category of Macedonian folk dances, which are typically performed in social or community settings. The dance is characterized by its specific spatial arrangement and the physical engagement of the participants. Dancers form a half-circle, a common configuration in regional oro traditions, which allows for a cohesive movement of the group while maintaining a connection between all participants. The dancers hold their hands up at the level of their shoulders, creating a unified line that moves in coordination with the rhythm of the music. The fundamental movement of Pembe involves steady, grounded steps performed on the whole foot. This provides a stable base for the dancers, which is then accented by a characteristic movement of the heels. This heel motion serves as a rhythmic and visual marker of the dance, distinguishing it from other regional oro variations. The structure of the dance is dynamic, defined by a progressive change in tempo. It begins at a slow, measured pace, allowing the dancers to establish the rhythm and the connection within the half-circle. As the dance progresses, the tempo gradually increases, leading to a faster, more energetic conclusion. This acceleration requires the dancers to maintain their coordination and the integrity of the half-circle formation while adapting to the changing speed of the music. The rhythm of the dance is set to a 2/4 meter, which provides the underlying pulse for the steps and the heel movements. Because the dance is a mixed-gender performance, it serves as a social activity that brings together different members of the community. The reliance on the whole foot for the basic steps ensures that the dance remains grounded, while the upward position of the arms adds a vertical dimension to the performance. The transition from slow to fast is a key element of the dance's narrative arc, requiring the dancers to be attentive to the music and to each other. While specific details regarding costumes, historical occasions, or notable figures are not described in the sources, the dance remains a recognized part of the Macedonian folk repertoire. It is a living tradition that reflects the regional characteristics of Veles, emphasizing both the technical precision of the heel movements and the communal nature of the circle dance. The simplicity of the 2/4 rhythm combined with the gradual increase in speed makes Pembe a distinct example of the Macedonian oro, requiring both stamina and rhythmic sensitivity from those who participate in the circle.

The dance was originally from the Empordà region, but started gaining popularity throughout Catalonia from the late 19th century to beginning of the 20th century after the modernisation done by Josep Maria Ventura i Casas.

thabal-chongba.name: Thabal Chongba
thabal-chongba.tagline: Manipuri Meitei moonlight circle dance during Yaoshang
thabal-chongba.profile: Thabal Chongba (Meitei: thabal = moonlight, chongba = dance) is a Manipuri folk dance in which young men and women join hands in concentric circles and dance under the moon, with rhythmic hopping steps, during the five-to-six-day Yaoshang festival (Manipur's spring festival coinciding with Holi) (Wikipedia, Dances of Manipur; Imphal Free Press). Traditionally performed in natural moonlight to folk songs accompanied by the pung drum and pena, it has long served as one of the few socially sanctioned occasions for young Meitei men and women to meet (Way2Barak; Imphal Free Press). Modern versions feature organised gatherings with bands playing drums, flutes and saxophones (Google Arts & Culture).
thabal-chongba.insight: Rooted in pre-Hindu Meitei society, the dance was elevated into a structured Yaoshang ritual after King Pamheiba adopted Gaudiya Vaishnavism around 1717, blending indigenous moonlight circle dances with Vaishnava devotion; it endures as a vehicle of community bonding and youth socialisation (Grokipedia; The Verandah Club).

chhau.name: Chhau
chhau.era: Roots in indigenous dance and martial practices; UNESCO-inscribed 2010
chhau.tagline: Eastern Indian masked martial dance of epics and ritual
chhau.profile: Chhau is a semi-classical Indian dance combining martial, tribal and folk traditions, found in three regional styles: Seraikella (Jharkhand), Purulia (West Bengal) and Mayurbhanj (Odisha), the first two using masks (Wikipedia). It enacts episodes from the Mahabharata, Ramayana and Puranas, local folklore and abstract themes, and is intimately connected to the spring festival Chaitra Parva (UNESCO). Its movement vocabulary includes mock combat (khel), stylized gaits of birds and animals, and movements based on village chores; it is traditionally performed by male troupes at night to reed pipes (mohuri, shehnai) and drums.
chhau.insight: Chhau was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2010, and the Sangeet Natak Akademi established a National Centre for Chhau Dance at Baripada, Odisha (Wikipedia).

war-dance.profile: A war dance is a dance involving mock combat, usually in reference to tribal warrior societies where such dances were performed as a ritual connected with endemic warfare. Martial arts in various cultures can be performed in dance-like settings for various reasons, such as for evoking ferocity in preparation for battle or showing off skill in a more stylized manner. It could also be for celebration of valor and conquest. Many such martial arts incorporate music, especially strong percussive rhythms.
war-dance.insight: A war dance is a dance involving mock combat, usually in reference to tribal warrior societies where such dances were performed as a ritual connected with endemic warfare.

worship-dance.profile: Worship dance or liturgical dance take on several forms of sacred dance in Christianity and Messianic Judaism, and is usually incorporated into liturgies or worship services. It has encountered controversy and even condemnations from church officials however.
