calinda.name: Calinda
calinda.country: Caribbean (Trinidad and Tobago, Haiti, Guadeloupe, Martinique), United States (Louisiana)
calinda.tagline: Caribbean martial art and war dance with African roots, practiced since the 1720s
calinda.profile: Calinda is a Caribbean martial art, folk music, and war dance originating in the 1720s from African combat dances brought by enslaved Africans. It is practiced notably in Trinidad and Tobago, Haiti, Guadeloupe, Martinique, and Louisiana. Calinda involves stick-fighting performed in ritualized arenas called gayelles, accompanied by call-and-response chants known as lavways, which evolved into calypso music.
calinda.insight: In 1894, Louisiana writer Kate Chopin referenced Calinda dance in her story 'La Belle Zoraïde,' highlighting Afro-Caribbean cultural presence in New Orleans.
sources: Source: Calinda on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calinda
calinda.profile_long:
Calinda, also spelled kalinda or kalenda, is a martial art, folk music, and war dance that emerged in the Caribbean during the 1720s. It was introduced by enslaved Africans brought through the transatlantic slave trade, rooted in combat dances from the Kingdom of Kongo. In Trinidad and Tobago, Calinda is recognized as the national martial art and is commonly practiced during Carnival, where stick-fighting contests take place in arenas called gayelles. These contests begin with ritual songs and ceremonies, including call-and-response chants called lavways, which historically cheered on the fighters and contributed to the development of modern calypso music. The dance and martial art were initially a form of entertainment and cultural expression for enslaved people, evolving alongside Carnival traditions brought by French planters and migrants from neighboring islands such as Grenada, Guadeloupe, Martinique, and Dominica.

Calinda's stick-fighting involves combatants known as boismen, who wear specific costumes and engage in ritualized fights that balance performance and martial skill. Despite the violent potential of stick-fighting, the dance form is widely practiced as a stylized performance. Annual Carnival competitions formalize these contests, preserving the martial art's combative roots. Similar stick-fighting traditions exist throughout the Caribbean, including l'agya, damaye, and mayolé in Guadeloupe and Martinique, and the Afro-Caribbean martial art Tire machèt in Haiti, which shares origins with Calinda. In Barbados, a related practice is called stick-licking or stick science, while in Puerto Rico, a comparable dance called Kokobalé is performed with Bomba music.

In Louisiana, Calinda was performed by Afro-Caribbean slaves and influenced local culture, as evidenced by the Cajun song "Allons danser Colinda" and literary references such as Kate Chopin's 1894 story "La Belle Zoraïde," which underscores the Afro-Caribbean presence in New Orleans. The dance was historically banned in some regions during the 19th century for being considered indecent but persisted in Haiti, Guadeloupe, and Louisiana. In Haiti, Calinda is still danced during Vodou ceremonies and celebrations, often mimicking combat movements with sticks and incorporating ritual elements.

The music accompanying Calinda is characterized by percussion instruments such as drums, bamboo drums (bamboula), banjos, and quills (reed pipes), creating rhythmic patterns that support the dancers' movements. The dance is performed in a circle, with musicians and spectators surrounding the fighters or dancers. The tempo is lively and energetic, matching the martial and performative aspects of the tradition. Calinda's enduring presence across the Caribbean and its diasporic communities reflects its significance as a cultural expression of African heritage, resistance, and identity.

devils-sword-dance.name: Devil's Sword Dance
devils-sword-dance.tagline: Demon-masked Buddhist sword dance of Kitakami
devils-sword-dance.profile: The Devil's Sword Dance (Onikenbai) is a folk sword dance handed down mainly in Kitakami and Oshu, Iwate Prefecture, in northeastern Japan, usually performed by a group of about eight dancers (Wikipedia, Devil's sword dance). Performers wear fierce oni (demon) masks that represent aspects of the Buddhist deity Fudo Myoo and dance dynamically with sword and fan to taiko drums, flute and kane, stomping and leaping; it is formally a type of Nenbutsu Kenbai performed as a prayer to ward off evil, comfort the dead and ensure good harvests (ANA; JeePe). Masks come in colours (red, blue, yellow, black, white) linked to directions and seasons.
devils-sword-dance.insight: Onikenbai was designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan in 1993 and, in November 2022, was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List as part of the collective 'Furyu-odori' listing (41 ritual dances from 24 prefectures) (JeePe; Nippon.com).

weapon-dance.profile: A weapon dance employs weapons—or stylized versions of weapons—traditionally used in combat in order to simulate, recall, or reenact combat or the moves of combat in the form of dance, usually for some ceremonial purpose. Such dancing is quite common to folk ritual in many parts of the world. Weapon dancing is certainly ancient; among the earliest historical references we have are those that refer to the pyrrhichios, a weapon dance in ancient Sparta, in which the dance was used as a kind of ritual training for battle. Related to weapon dances and war dances is the dance of the hunt.

atsiagbekor.tagline: Ewe war dance, modern variant of Agbekor/Atamga
atsiagbekor.profile: Atsiagbekor is a traditional war dance of the Ewe people, originating in Ghana's Volta Region and extending to Togo and Benin (Wikipedia). It traces to the war dance Atamga and was historically performed in platoon formations reflecting reconnaissance, surprise attacks and combat maneuvers, with the Atimavu master drum leading an ensemble of drummers, dancers and singers. Today it is performed at social gatherings, festivals and educational institutions, notably by the Ghana Dance Ensemble at the University of Ghana (Wikipedia).
atsiagbekor.insight: Educational centers such as the Dagbe Cultural Center in Kopeyia teach Atsiagbekor, and the Ghana Dance Ensemble has showcased it on global stages (Wikipedia).

theyyannam.name: Theyyannam
theyyannam.tagline: A ritual folk dance from Kerala depicting the cycle of paddy cultivation.
theyyannam.profile: Theyyannam is a traditional ritual folk art form practiced by the Pulaya, Kurava, and Paraya communities in the central Travancore region of Kerala, India. The dance serves as a symbolic representation of the agricultural cycle, specifically paddy cultivation. It is primarily performed in areas such as Mavelikkara and Pandalam within the Alappuzha district.
theyyannam.insight: In the paddy fields of central Travancore, eight men and a group of women perform the entire agricultural cycle—from ploughing to threshing—as a ritual dance to the rhythm of the harmonium, idakka, and tabla.
sources: Source: Theyyannam on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theyyannam
theyyannam.profile_long: Theyyannam is a ritual folk art form deeply rooted in the agricultural traditions of the central Travancore region in Kerala, India. The dance is specifically associated with the Pulaya, Kurava, and Paraya communities, who have historically maintained this tradition. Geographically, the practice is concentrated in Mavelikkara, Pandalam, and other parts of the Alappuzha district. The dance functions as a narrative performance of the agricultural process, specifically focusing on paddy cultivation. The performance is structured around the various stages of farming, beginning with the preparation of the land. Eight men initiate the ritual by ploughing a paddy field and planting seedlings. The narrative progresses as women enter the field, bringing breakfast for the men, and subsequently join them in the planting process. The performance continues to represent the growth, harvesting, and threshing of the crop, with the participants working together to mimic the full cycle of cultivation. The musical accompaniment is integral to the performance, utilizing the harmonium, idakka, and tabla to provide the rhythmic foundation for the dancers. As a ritual art form, it reflects the connection between the community and their labor, transforming the physical acts of farming into a structured, rhythmic, and communal event. The tradition remains a living practice within its specific cultural communities in Kerala.
theyyannam.sacred_note: The dance is described as a ritual folk art form associated with specific communities and agricultural cycles; outsiders should observe with respect for its ritual significance.

thidambu-nritham.name: Thidambu Nritham
thidambu-nritham.tagline: Kerala temple dance carrying the deity's image on the head
thidambu-nritham.profile: Thidambu Nritham is a Hindu temple ritual dance of North Malabar and Kasaragod district, Kerala, in which the dancer carries the 'thidambu' - the decorated image or replica of the deity, built on a bamboo frame - aloft on his head while performing rhythmic footwork to chenda drumming (Wikipedia; Kerala Tourism). It is performed mainly by Namboothiri Brahmins (occasionally by other Brahmin communities), is believed to be six to seven centuries old, and follows Natyashastra principles (Wikipedia). The performer wears a pleated skirt, silk vest, ornaments and a decorated turban; a full staging involves about ten people, including seven musicians and two lamp-bearers, and is associated with annual temple festivals, notably in Kannur (Kerala Tourism).
thidambu-nritham.insight: The dance fuses devotion and discipline: balancing the heavy deity-image on the head while dancing transforms the performer into a living vehicle of the divine, and it is staged as part of temple festivals across North Malabar (Kerala Tourism; academic study, Neliti).

This art form is performed by the artists of malaya (the artist who recognised for performing the art form called as a "perumalayan") community. This art is performed during Utsavam (annual temple festival). Clan deities such as Bhagavathi, Shiva are worshipped in these forms. It is usually celebrated from mid-December to mid-March, for a duration of 2–3 days in different temples, varying from temple to temple.

otole-dance.name: Otole dance
otole-dance.tagline: A traditional war dance of the Acholi people of Northern Uganda.
otole-dance.profile: The Otole is a traditional war dance of the Acholi people of Northern Uganda, historically serving as a method of pre-combat training and community mobilization. It features mock battles, strategic attack and retreat movements, and victory celebrations, all designed to instill courage and transmit martial traditions. Today, the dance persists in cultural festivals and heritage showcases, where it serves as a living link to Acholi history and identity.
otole-dance.insight: The Otole is a war dance of the Acholi people where men in leopard skins and ostrich feathers perform mock combat, while women flank them in a procession to symbolize the community's collective defense.
sources: Source: Otole dance on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otole_dance
otole-dance.profile_long:
The Otole dance is an integral component of the cultural heritage of the Acholi people in Northern Uganda. Historically, the dance functioned as a vital tool for martial preparation, serving as a form of pre-combat training that conditioned warriors for the physical and psychological demands of warfare. Through the performance of mock battles, stimulated attack and retreat movements, and victory dances, the community was able to galvanize support for proposed combat and commemorate past victories. The dance was organized at the call of a chief, acting as a mechanism for community mobilization and the transmission of oral history from elders to younger generations.

The visual presentation of the Otole is distinct, characterized by specific attire and symbolic props. Men participating in the dance traditionally wear leopard skins and ostrich feathers, while carrying horns, shields, and spears to represent their role as protectors. Women, who play a crucial role in the performance, carry small wooden axes or unsharpened sticks. The structure of the dance involves a specific spatial arrangement: women form a procession that is flanked by men, a formation that symbolizes the male responsibility to protect both the women and the broader community. The performance is initiated by a lead woman singer who performs 'kigila', or ululations, followed by the lead man who begins the 'owoc', or mock fight.

Beyond its martial origins, the Otole carries significant social and symbolic weight. It reinforces gender roles, courage, and collective identity among the Acholi people. The dance serves as a form of dramatized combat that educates the community about defense and historical memory. In contemporary times, the traditional martial functions of the Otole have largely faded due to changes in social organization and governance. However, the dance remains a living tradition, persisting as part of cultural demonstrations and heritage events. It is frequently performed alongside other traditional Acholi dances, such as the Bwola (a royal dance) and the Larakaraka (a courtship dance), in cultural showcases. During these modern performances, elders often execute traditional moves with spears and shields to evoke historical memory and community pride, ensuring that the essence of the Otole continues to be recognized and valued by new generations.

reggada.name: Reggada
reggada.tagline: Morocco's Rif Berber dance — shoulders rolling, rifles raised in air, the celebration dance of the Riffi mountain communities.
reggada.profile: Reggada is a traditional dance and musical genre of Morocco specific to the Amazigh tribes of the north-east (provinces of Oujda, Berkane and Taourirt).
reggada.insight: Reggada has crossed from rural Rif weddings into mainstream Moroccan and Algerian pop music — modern artists like Cheb Mimoun el-Oujdi and Stati have made reggada one of the most-played styles at urban celebrations from Casablanca to Marseille's Moroccan diaspora. The dance's signature shoulder roll has been borrowed into raï and modern fusion across the Maghreb.

kandeka.name: Kandeka
kandeka.tagline: Kunene stick-fighting and slap-boxing ringed by song
kandeka.profile: Kandeka (also Khandeka) is a martial tradition of the Kunene people of southern Angola encompassing stick-fighting, slap-boxing and a war-dance display, documented by M. Thomas J. Desch-Obi (Wikipedia). At parties and festivals, particularly before engolo matches, public ritual slap-boxing took place in dance circles: an outer ring of community members kept a clapped rhythm and call-and-response song while fighters entered, raising open hands as a challenge. António Nogueira described kandeka stick duels among the Humbe in the 1850s as a means of conflict resolution.
kandeka.insight: Kandeka is cited as one of the Angolan combat-dance traditions (with engolo) from which Afro-Brazilian capoeira is believed to derive, illustrating how martial movement, music and dance circles travelled the Atlantic with enslaved Angolans.

dirk-dance.name: Dirk dance
dirk-dance.tagline: Indonesia, 1841 — Scottish dance performed while brandishing a dirk
dirk-dance.profile: A dirk dance is a Scottish dance performed while brandishing a dirk. It is a solo dance but can be performed by two or more people dancing in unison. The dance is quite different in style from the better known Highland dances and in many ways imitates the use of a dirk in fighting. Research suggests that the dance may, in fact, have originated as a series of moves for training in the use of the dirk. There are records showing that a Dirk Dance was included in Highland Dance competitions in 1841. The dance was recorded by J. F. and T. M.
dirk-dance.insight: One version of the dance involved attacking and defensive techniques with single-sticks and targe shields and was last performed in Britain in 1850 by two brothers named MacLennan, one of whom was a colleague of Mr Mather.

khattak-dance.name: Khattak Dance
khattak-dance.tagline: The Pashtun sword dance — Khattak warriors swing live blades while spinning in tight formation.
khattak-dance.profile: The Khattak (Pashto: خټک اتڼ [xaˈʈak], Urdu: رقص خٹک Khattak attan) is a swift martial attan dance usually performed while carrying a sword and a handkerchief (while not always are they holding a sword and handkerchief) by the tribesmen from the agile Khattak tribe of Pashtuns. Khattak dance is also a national dance of Pakistan. It was performed by Khattak warriors before going to wars in the time of Malik Shahbaz Khan Khattak and then Khushal Khan Khattak. It was used as a war-preparation exercise and is known to be the only dance with swordplay.
khattak-dance.insight: The Khattak Dance traces directly to the 17th-century military training of Pashtun warriors under Khushal Khan Khattak — the poet-warrior chief who used the dance to keep his fighters in combat condition during peacetime. The most advanced variant involves spinning three live swords simultaneously around the head, neck, and waist; it is taught father-to-son in Pashtun families across Pakistan and the Afghan border.

ohafia-war-dance.name: Ohafia War Dance
ohafia-war-dance.tagline: A traditional Igbo war dance from Nigeria commemorating historical martial prowess.
ohafia-war-dance.profile: The Ohafia War Dance, known in Igbo as ikpirikpi ogu, is a traditional performance originating from the Ohafia region of Eastern Nigeria. It serves as a commemoration of the strength and martial history of the Ohafia people, who were historically renowned as warriors. The dance is performed by men who mimic the actions of battle, including the ritualistic beheading of enemies, to celebrate both collective history and individual achievements.
ohafia-war-dance.insight: The lead dancer of the Ohafia War Dance carries a basket of human skulls, known as oyaya, while holding a cutlass and a palm shoot in his mouth to signify the warrior heritage of the Ohafia people.
sources: Source: Ohafia War Dance on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohafia_War_Dance
ohafia-war-dance.profile_long:
The Ohafia War Dance, or ikpirikpi ogu, is a significant cultural performance rooted in the history of the Ohafia people of Eastern Nigeria. Historically, the Ohafia ancestors were recognized as mighty men of war, and their warrior tradition remains a fundamental aspect of their identity. This identity is deeply connected to the practice of ikpirikpi ogu, which historically involved the beheading of a fallen enemy as proof of a man's courage and strength. 

In the past, this martial requirement was the gateway to the Ogbu-Isi society. Only those who successfully brought home a human head were permitted to join this society and wear an eagle's plume, which served as a visible symbol of their bravery. Today, the dance is performed by a group of muscular men to commemorate the strength and success of their ancestors in past wars. 

The performance is structured around a lead dancer who carries a basket full of human skulls, referred to as oyaya. This lead dancer also carries a short cutlass and holds a small palm shoot in his mouth. Surrounding him, fellow dancers are dressed as fierce warriors. These dancers perform movements that mime the act of cutting off human heads, effectively portraying Ohafia as a land of brave warriors. The performance is accompanied by music played on the akwatankwa instrument. Beyond its historical roots, the dance is also utilized to celebrate the achievements of individuals within the community. Due to the limited available documentation, specific details regarding the choreography, footwork, and musical structure remain largely unrecorded in current sources.

hoko.name: Hoko
hoko.tagline: term used to refer to the tribal war dance of Easter Island
hoko.profile: Hoko is a term used to refer to the tribal war dance of Easter Island. However, it is also performed as a welcome dance and a gesture of hospitality, and it is performed before sports matches in the same way that the haka is performed by the New Zealand national rugby union team, similar to those in Samoa, Tonga and Fiji.
hoko.insight: Hoko is a term used to refer to the tribal war dance of Easter Island.

sagayan.name: Sagayan
sagayan.tagline: Philippines — Philippine war dance performed by Maguindanao, Maranao, and Iranun depicting in dramatic fashion the steps …
sagayan.profile: Sagayan is a Philippine war dance performed by Maguindanao, Maranao, and Iranun depicting in dramatic fashion the steps their hero, Prince Bantugan, took upon wearing his armaments, the war he fought in and his subsequent victory afterwards. Performers, depicting fierce warriors, would carry shields with shell noisemakers in one hand and a kampilan sword on the other. Dancers of the Sagayan wear atypical costumes based on mythological descriptions of Bantugan's equipment in the epic Darangen.
sagayan.insight: Sagayan is a Philippine war dance performed by Maguindanao, Maranao, and Iranun depicting in dramatic fashion the steps their hero, Prince Bantugan, took upon wearing his armaments, the war he fought in and his subsequent victory afterwards.
sources: Source: Sagayan on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sagayan
sagayan.sacred_note: Not described in sources as sacred, though it is deeply connected to the epic Darangen.

khorumi.name: Khorumi
khorumi.profile: Khorumi is a war dance originating in Adjara (sometimes attributed to neighbouring Guria) in southwestern Georgia, rooted in the country's many invasions (Wikipedia; geofolk.ge). Originally performed by only a few men, today's version sees thirty or forty dancers participate, with the rules requiring the number to be odd. It has four parts: searching for a campsite, reconnoitering the enemy camp, the fight, and the victory celebration. Unusually, it is accompanied only by instruments - the doli (drum) and chiboni (bagpipe) - never by clapping, and uses a distinctive five-beat (3+2) meter. Some scholars link it to dances of ancient Georgian tribes described by Xenophon.
khorumi.insight: Khorumi was named a Monument of Intangible Cultural Heritage of Georgia in 2013 and has become a template for the performance of Georgian military skill; in 2024-25 it was adopted by pro-EU protesters in Tbilisi as a dance of peaceful resistance (Georgia Today; geofolk.ge).

kabasaran.name: Kabasaran
kabasaran.era: Pre-colonial Minahasan warrior tradition; refined in the colonial era
kabasaran.tagline: Minahasan warrior dance of fierce red-clad fighters
kabasaran.profile: Kabasaran is a traditional Minahasan martial art and war dance from North Sulawesi, performed by men clad in red costumes wielding a sword (santi) with a shield, or a spear (wengkouw) (Wikipedia). The dancers, called kawasalan ('imitating fighting cocks'), are drawn from the hereditary Waranei (warrior) lineage. The word derives from kawasalan, related to the Moluccan Sakalele/Cakalele dance, which was simplified and combined with quadrille moves to create a dance suitable for welcoming Dutch guests. The basic structure uses nine sword or spear movements; dancers wear feathered headdresses and red woven cloth, with fierce wide-eyed expressions.
kabasaran.insight: Historians describe Kabasaran as a refinement of the rougher cakalele, deliberately softened with European quadrille movements to make it acceptable as a colonial welcoming dance (Hello Indonesia, citing Sutisno Kutoyo).

huiyen-lallong.name: Huyen Lallong
huiyen-lallong.era: Ancient (recorded in Puya manuscripts; revived 20th c.)
huiyen-lallong.tagline: Manipuri martial art of sword and spear, also called Thang-Ta
huiyen-lallong.profile: Huyen Langlon (Meitei: huyen = war, langlon/lanlong = art/knowledge) is the martial-art-and-dance tradition of the Meitei people of Manipur, comprising Thang-Ta (armed combat, from thang = sword and ta = spear) and Sarit Sarak (unarmed combat) (Wikipedia, Huyen langlon). Its spectacular component includes the thangkairol (sword dance) and khousarol (spear dance), practised in ritual, demonstration and combat modes, and is closely intertwined with Manipuri ritual and classical dance (Wikipedia). The tradition's earliest records appear in Puya manuscripts such as the Chainarol-Puya; it was suppressed under British rule (1891-1947) and later revived (Wikipedia).
huiyen-lallong.insight: The art's continuity was sustained by masters such as Gurumayum Gourakishor Sharma, who received the Padma Shri in 2009, underscoring its formal recognition as a living martial-cultural heritage of Manipur (Wikipedia).

hooping.name: Hooping
hooping.tagline: manipulation of and artistic movement or dancing with a hoop (or hoops)
hooping.profile: Hooping (also called hula hooping or hoop dance) is the manipulation of and artistic movement or dancing with a hoop (or hoops). Hoops can be made of metal, wood, or plastic. Hooping combines technical moves and tricks with freestyle or technical dancing. Hooping can be practiced to or performed with music. In contrast to the classic toy hula hoop, modern hoopers use heavier and larger diameter hoops, and frequently rotate the hoop around parts of the body other than the waist, including the hips, chest, neck, shoulders, thighs, knees, arms, hands, thumbs, feet, and toes.
hooping.insight: In March 2013, the largest hula hoop workout (407 participants) was achieved at Ravenscraig Regional Sports Facility in Scotland by North Lanarkshire Leisure and Powerhoop Fitness.
sources: Source: Hooping on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hooping

fancy-dance.name: Fancy dance
fancy-dance.tagline: Athletic Native American powwow dance of Ponca origin
fancy-dance.profile: Fancy dance (Fancy Feather or Fancy War Dance) is a competitive powwow dance of Native American communities, widely credited to Ponca dancer Gus McDonald, who developed it in Oklahoma in the 1920s-1930s and was the first World Champion Fancy Dancer (Wikipedia; National Cowboy & Western Heritage Museum). It arose after U.S. authorities suppressed traditional dances under the 1883 Code of Indian Offenses, when tribes created new public-friendly dances also performed at Wild West shows. It is highly athletic - spins, high kicks, leaps - with dancers in vivid regalia featuring two large feather bustles, beaded harness, roach headdress and bells; dancers must strike a pose when the drumbeat stops. Women's fancy shawl dance developed later (PowWows.com; Britannica).
fancy-dance.insight: This row was mis-filed under India / South Asia: Fancy dance is NOT a South Asian dance but a Native American powwow dance, so the country is corrected to the United States (Smithsonian Center for Folklife; Oklahoma Historical Society).

shalako.name: Shalako
shalako.tagline: United States, 1990 — series of dances and ceremonies conducted by the Native American Zuni people for the Zuni people at the win…
shalako.profile: Shalako is a series of dances and ceremonies conducted by the Native American Zuni people for the Zuni people at the winter solstice, typically following the harvest. The Shalako ceremony and feast has been closed to non-native peoples since 1990. However, non-native peoples may be invited as guests by a Zuni tribal member. Nancy Bonvillain described the Shalakos, "They brought good fortune, abundant crops, and many children." They are chosen at Winter Solstice, when they begin to learn the chants they will recite in the early December ceremony.
shalako.insight: Shalako is a series of dances and ceremonies conducted by the Native American Zuni people for the Zuni people at the winter solstice, typically following the harvest.
sources: Source: Shalako on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shalako

scottish-sword-dances.name: Scottish sword dances
scottish-sword-dances.tagline: Spain, 15th century — The Sword dance is one of the best known of all Highland dances, an ancient dance of war
scottish-sword-dances.profile: The Sword dance is one of the best known of all Highland dances, an ancient dance of war. Performance of sword dances in the folklore of Scotland is recorded from as early as the 15th century. Related customs are found in the Welsh and English Morris dance, in Austria, Germany, Flanders, France, Italy, Spain, Portugal and Romania. In Ghillie Callum or "Scottish sword dance" the dancer crosses two swords on the ground in an "X" or a "+" shape, and dances around and within the 4 quarters of it. The dirk dance involves either one or two dancers, each holding a single dirk.
scottish-sword-dances.insight: According to these beliefs, Noah, upon first drinking fermented wine, crossed two vines and danced above them while Gillidh Callum played the bagpipes, thus inventing the ancestor of the Highland sword dance (gillie callum).
sources: Source: Scottish sword dances on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_sword_dances

jingle-dress.name: Jingle dress
jingle-dress.tagline: Ojibwe healing powwow dance - MISFILED under India
jingle-dress.profile: The Jingle Dress Dance is a First Nations and Native American women's powwow dance and regalia tradition of the Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) peoples of the Great Lakes region, NOT a South Asian dance (Wikipedia, Jingle dress; Parks Canada). Its origin is attributed to Ojibwe communities - Mille Lacs, the Red Lake Band of Chippewa and Whitefish Bay (Naotkamegwanning) - through a recurring dream given to a Midewinini (medicine man) whose gravely ill granddaughter was healed by dancing in a dress adorned with rows of metal cones (ziibaaska'iganan) (Wikipedia). University of Minnesota professor Brenda Child dates the dress and dance to circa 1918-19, tied to the 1918-19 influenza pandemic; it arose just as the U.S. Indian Office issued a circular banning ritual dancing (1921) (Univ. of Minnesota).
jingle-dress.insight: Far from a 'party trick,' the jingle dress is a sacred healing tradition - dancers keep one foot connected to the earth and the sound of the cones is believed to carry prayers; it became an official powwow category after being popularised by Maggie White of Naotkamegwanning from the late 1960s (Parks Canada).

grass-dance.name: Grass dance
grass-dance.tagline: United States — style of modern Native American men's pow wow dancing originating in the warrior societies on the Northern …
grass-dance.profile: The grass dance or Omaha dance is a style of modern Native American men's pow wow dancing originating in the warrior societies on the Northern Great Plains. Unlike most forms of pow wow dancing, the grass dance regalia generally has no feathers besides the occasional roach feather. The regalia consists of brightly colored fringe made of either yarn, broadcloth, or ribbon.
grass-dance.insight: When he shared this vision with his village, the use of his legs was returned to him and he performed the first grass dance.
sources: Source: Grass dance on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grass_dance
grass-dance.sacred_note: Historically, the dance was a ritual for healing and blessing the ground, not for entertainment; practitioners should respect its origins and the protocols of the specific First Nations or tribes hosting the event.

ojibwe-drum-dance.name: Ojibwe drum dance
ojibwe-drum-dance.tagline: A sacred tradition involving the 'dream drum' introduced to the Ojibwe in the 1870s.
ojibwe-drum-dance.profile: The Ojibwe drum dance is a sacred practice centered on the 'dream drum', an instrument held in high regard and often treated as a living being. Rooted in an origin story involving Tailfeather Woman, the tradition emerged in the 1870s and is closely linked to the grass dance. The dance is organized through societies consisting of a drum owner, singers, and other participants.
ojibwe-drum-dance.insight: In the 1870s, a Sioux woman known as Tailfeather Woman introduced the sacred 'dream drum' to the Ojibwe, an instrument often treated as a living entity within the drum dance society.
sources: Source: Drum dance on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drum_dance
ojibwe-drum-dance.profile_long: The Ojibwe drum dance is a distinct cultural and spiritual practice centered on the use of a specific instrument known as the 'dream drum'. This drum is not merely an object but is considered sacred, often treated by practitioners as a living thing. The history of the dance is tied to a specific origin narrative involving a Sioux woman identified as Tailfeather Woman or Turkey Tailfeather Woman, who is credited with bringing the drum to the Ojibwe people. According to ethnomusicologist Thomas Vennum, this narrative is historically accurate, with the events likely occurring during the 1870s, a date specifically corroborated by researcher Elaine Keillor as 1877. Anthropological consensus suggests that the Ojibwe drum dance, while rooted in this specific origin story, shares a lineage with the grass dance. The performance and maintenance of the tradition are managed by drum dance societies, which are structured groups composed of a drum owner, singers, and other members. These societies serve as the custodians of the dance and the drum itself. While the drum dance is a significant cultural marker, the specific technical movements, footwork, and choreographic structures are not described in the sources. The tradition remains a subject of study for its social and spiritual significance within Ojibwe communities, reflecting a complex relationship between the music, the instrument, and the societal roles of those who participate.
ojibwe-drum-dance.sacred_note: The drum used for the dance is considered sacred and may be treated as a living thing.

native-american-hoop-dance.name: Native American Hoop Dance
native-american-hoop-dance.tagline: United States, 1930 — form of individual dance, performed as a show dance in many tribes
native-american-hoop-dance.profile: Native American Hoop Dance is a form of individual dance, performed as a show dance in many tribes. It features a solo dancer dancing with a dozen or more hoops and using them to form a variety of both static and dynamic shapes (poses and moves). Most of the hoop dances in tribes across North America belong to modern hoop dance, which was invented in 1930.
native-american-hoop-dance.insight: The first World Hoop Dance Competition was held at the New Mexico State Fair in 1991.
sources: Source: Native American Hoop Dance on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_American_Hoop_Dance

yowlah.name: Yowlah
yowlah.tagline: A traditional martial dance of the UAE and Oman, simulating battle and victory.
yowlah.profile: Yowlah, also known as Al-Ayyala, is a traditional martial dance originating from Bedouin war traditions in the United Arab Emirates and Oman. It involves rhythmic chanting, drum music, and the manipulation of sticks, swords, or dummy rifles to simulate battle scenes. The dance is performed at weddings, national festivals, and official ceremonies, serving as a symbol of tribal unity and national identity. It was inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2014.
yowlah.insight: On 26 November 2010, 285 participants from three different tribes performed the largest Yowlah dance in Fujairah to celebrate before the Crown Prince.
sources: Source: Yowlah on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yowlah
yowlah.profile_long: The Yowlah, frequently referred to as Al-Ayyala, is a foundational martial performance art practiced across the United Arab Emirates and the Sultanate of Oman. Historically, the dance emerged as a Bedouin war ritual, performed to celebrate victory after tribal conflicts or the successful return of pearl-diving expeditions. Today, it serves as a vital expression of national identity, performed during weddings, national holidays, state visits, and even football matches. The dance is characterized by its simulation of a battle scene, where performers embody the values of defense, solidarity, and triumph. In 2014, the art form was recognized by UNESCO as part of the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, a status intended to facilitate the transfer of skills and values between generations. The performance structure typically involves two rows of approximately twenty men facing one another. These men carry thin bamboo sticks, which represent spears or swords, though dummy rifles made of wood and metal or real weapons may also be used. Between these rows, musicians provide a rhythmic foundation using large and small drums, tambourines, brass cymbals, leather bagpipes, and flutes. The rows of men move their heads and sticks in synchronization with the drum rhythm while chanting poetic lyrics that glorify nomadic life and tribal virtues. In the United Arab Emirates, women often participate by standing at the front of the performance, engaging in the 'naash' ritual, which involves tossing their long hair from side to side as a gesture of gratitude for the protection offered by the male dancers. The melody of the accompanying music is noted for having seven tones in an irregular, repeated pattern, with the specific poetry varying depending on the occasion. The role of the lead performer is often inherited and carries the responsibility of training new participants. While the Yowlah is inclusive of all ages and social classes, regional variations exist, such as the Razfah, the Ardah, and the more rural al-wahabbiyya, which may exclude female participation. In modern contexts, the Yowlah has transitioned into the competitive sphere, notably through the Al Meydan reality series and the Shaikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Championship, which have helped elevate the dance's profile among younger generations.

takalo.name: Takalo
takalo.profile: The takalo is a Niuean war dance. Performed by an individual warrior or group of warriors, the dance is a formal challenge, and was traditionally performed prior to engaging the enemy with traditional war clubs. In modern times, the takalo is often performed prior to a rugby game or winning a game of some sport code. The takalo is also performed to welcome dignitaries upon arrival into Niue, and signifies that the dignitaries' arrival is for the purpose of peace and harmony.
takalo.insight: The takalo is a Niuean war dance.
sources: Source: Takalo on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takalo

velakali.name: Velakali
velakali.tagline: Nair martial temple dance enacting a Pandava-Kaurava battle
velakali.profile: Velakali is an all-male martial temple dance of the Nair (traditional warrior) community of Kerala, in which performers wear the costume and colourful headgear of medieval Nair soldiers and wield swords and shields, with movements drawn from the martial art Kalarippayattu (Kerala Tourism; Wikidata). It depicts a battle between the Pandavas and Kauravas and originated in the princely state of Chempakassery (modern Ambalappuzha) under army chieftain Mathur Panicker (Kerala Tourism). It is a regular feature of the pooram at the Ambalappuzha Sree Krishna Temple and marks the start of the annual Painkuni festival at the Sree Padmanabhaswamy Temple, Thiruvananthapuram, accompanied by panchavadyam percussion (Kerala Tourism; Parampara Project).
velakali.insight: Velakali preserves the martial heritage of Kerala's Nair militias within a devotional temple frame, transforming choreographed swordplay into ritual offering at major temple festivals (Kerala Tourism).

aragonaise.name: Aragonaise
aragonaise.tagline: Spain — In a musical context, an Aragonaise (literally a person or thing from Aragon, a region in Spain) is a "danc…
aragonaise.profile: In a musical context, an Aragonaise (literally a person or thing from Aragon, a region in Spain) is a "dance of Aragon". This is a driving triple metre dance which is traditionally accompanied by guitars, castanets and hand clapping. There are two famous musical compositions named "Aragonaise", one by Jules Massenet from his opera Le Cid, the other from the entr'acte to act 4 of the opera Carmen by Georges Bizet.
aragonaise.insight: In a musical context, an Aragonaise (literally a person or thing from Aragon, a region in Spain) is a "dance of Aragon".

alegras.name: Alegrías
alegras.tagline: A festive flamenco dance from Cádiz, Spain, characterized by a 12-beat rhythmic cycle.
alegras.profile: Alegrías is a foundational flamenco palo originating in Cádiz, Spain, known for its festive character and rigorous structural requirements. It belongs to the cantiñas family, defined by a 12-beat rhythmic cycle that emphasizes beats 3, 6, 8, 10, and 12. Traditionally performed with a blend of grace and technical precision, the dance follows a specific sequence including a salida, paseo, silencio, castellana, zapateado, and bulerías.
alegras.insight: Emerging from the 19th-century occupation of Cádiz, this dance preserves the rhythmic ghost of the Aragonese jota within the strict, high-speed architecture of the flamenco palo.
sources: Source: Alegrías on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alegr%C3%ADas
alegras.profile_long:
The Alegrías is a cornerstone of the flamenco tradition, originating in the coastal city of Cádiz during the French occupation and the era of the Cortes de Cádiz. It is classified as a cante chico, a category of flamenco known for its festive and lighthearted nature. The dance is believed to have evolved from the Aragonese jota, which took root in Cádiz and was later adapted into the flamenco style by the singer Enrique Butrón. The characteristic vocal refrain, 'tiriti, tran, tran...', was introduced by Ignacio Espeleta, becoming a hallmark of the form. Historically, the Alegrías served as a primary festive dance in the 19th-century cafés cantantes, though its popularity shifted in the 20th century with the rise of other forms like the tango flamenco and bulería.

Musically, the Alegrías is structured around a 12-beat cycle, sharing a rhythmic foundation with the soleá but performed at a significantly faster tempo, typically between 120 and 170 beats per minute. The emphasis falls on beats 3, 6, 8, 10, and 12. While the song can be performed alone, the traditional dance is one of the most structurally rigid forms in flamenco. A complete performance must include a specific sequence of sections: the salida (entrance), the paseo (walkaround), the silencio (a slower, adagio-like section), the castellana (an upbeat transition), the zapateado (intricate footwork), and a concluding bulerías. This structure ensures a narrative arc that moves from an initial entrance to complex rhythmic displays.

Technically, the dance is demanding, requiring a high degree of coordination between the upper and lower body. Dancers must exhibit fluid arm movements and graceful carriage while executing precise, soft footwork. The aesthetic is traditionally feminine, though it is performed by all genders. Dancers typically wear ankle-length dresses adorned with ruffles, lace, and ribbons, often accompanied by a bata de cola (a dress with a long train). Accessories such as mantillas, flowers, combs, and coral earrings complete the look. Today, the tradition is maintained through performance and competition, most notably the annual National Competition of Alegrías held in Cádiz. The form remains a living tradition, with its evolution documented through the work of historical figures like Enrique el Mellizo and modern practitioners who continue to refine its technical and expressive boundaries.

straight-dance.name: Straight dance
straight-dance.era: developed 20th c. from older war dances
straight-dance.tagline: Southern Plains Native American men's powwow dance — NOT Chinese
straight-dance.profile: The Straight Dance (Southern Straight / Southern Traditional) is a style of Native American powwow dancing from the Southern Plains tribes of Oklahoma, attributed to the Ponca Hethushka war society (English Wikipedia). A dignified 'gentleman's dance,' it recounts a hunting or war party tracking an enemy, using a measured toe-heel step danced clockwise. Regalia includes a ribbon shirt, otter dragger, roach headdress and beadwork.
straight-dance.insight: It is a formal, prestigious expression of Southern Plains warrior heritage that preserved war-society traditions after those societies dissolved (English Wikipedia; PowWows.com).

kromanti-dance.name: Kromanti dance
kromanti-dance.tagline: Jamaican Maroon possession ceremony of Akan (Coromantee) origin
kromanti-dance.profile: Kromanti dance (Kromanti Play) is a Jamaican Maroon religious ceremony rooted in traditional African music and religious practices, especially those of the Akan people of Ghana (Wikipedia). The name derives from Kormantin, a historical slave fort on the Ghanaian coast. The ceremony invokes ancestral spirits through specialized drumming (gumbe, apinti), songs in the ritual Kromanti language (a creolized Akan dialect) and possession dances, led by a ritual specialist (fete-man/myal-man) (Wikipedia; Caribbean Languages).
kromanti-dance.insight: Ethnographer Kenneth Bilby's fieldwork documented spirit songs specific to individual ancestors, showing Kromanti invocations operate independently of later-adopted Christianity; the broader Maroon Heritage of Moore Town was proclaimed a UNESCO Masterpiece in 2003 and inscribed on the Representative List in 2008 (Caribbean Languages; UNESCO ICH).

chennu-nalike.name: Chennu Nalike
chennu-nalike.tagline: Tulu Mera-community post-harvest ritual dance of Suggi
chennu-nalike.profile: Chennu Nalike is an ancient traditional folk-ritual art practised by the Mera (Moger/Mogera) community of Tulu Nadu, an indigenous, matrilineally organised people of Kasaragod (Kerala) and the Mangalore, Udupi and Coorg districts of Karnataka (Wikipedia). Performed at night after the harvest in the Tulu month of Suggi (around February-March), it begins on Suggi Punnam (full moon) and lasts three to nine days as decided by the community head (Wikipedia). It features two characters, Chennu and Koraga; the Chennu wears a woman's costume with a Sampige flower on the head, while men and women provide background music and sing Paddanas (Tuluva oral epics) (Wikipedia).
chennu-nalike.insight: The Mera belong to the body of Tuluva ritual specialists (alongside Nalike, Parava and Pambada communities) who serve as mediums in Bhuta Kola spirit worship, situating Chennu Nalike within the wider Dravidian ritual cosmology of Tulu Nadu (Wikipedia, Buta Kola).

balinese-dance.name: Balinese dance
balinese-dance.tagline: Umbrella tradition of Bali's sacred and secular dances
balinese-dance.profile: Balinese dance is an ancient tradition central to the religious and artistic expression of the Balinese people, characterized by dynamic, angular and intensely expressive movement of fingers, hands, head and eyes (Wikipedia). This is the umbrella/parent category encompassing specific dances such as legong, baris, kecak and the ritual Sanghyang Dedari. Most are connected to Balinese Hindu or animist ritual. UNESCO classifies traditional Balinese dance into three genres: Wali (sacred temple dances), Bebali (semi-sacred ceremonial dances) and Balih-balihan (secular entertainment dances).
balinese-dance.insight: The three genres of traditional dance in Bali - represented by nine dances including Rejang, Sanghyang Dedari, Baris Upacara, Topeng Sidakarya, Gambuh, Wayang Wong and Legong - were inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List on 2 December 2015 (10.COM, Windhoek, Namibia) (UNESCO; Jakarta Post).

barachum.name: Barachum (Talchum)
barachum.tagline: Korean Buddhist cymbal dance of the Yeongsanjae rite
barachum.profile: Barachum is a representative Korean Buddhist ritual dance (jakbeop) performed by Buddhist monks with bara, cymbal-like brass instruments (Wikipedia). Composed of splendid and complex movements, performers step back and forth or revolve in agile action; its purpose is to expel evil spirits and purify the mind and the sacred space. It is performed as part of the Yeongsanjae Buddhist ceremony alongside the butterfly dance (Nabichum) and drum dance (Beopgochum), invoking mantras to ward off impurities.
barachum.insight: Barachum is one of the principal dances of Yeongsanjae, the Korean Buddhist Lotus Sutra re-enactment inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List in 2009; it sets a solemn, disciplined tone early in the rite (Wikipedia: Yeongsanjae; UNESCO).

angama.name: Angama
angama.tagline: Masked ancestral spirits visit homes during Yaeyama Obon
angama.profile: Angama is an Obon ancestral-spirit ritual dance of Japan's Yaeyama Islands (Ishigaki and neighbouring islands). Troupes led by two masked elders - Ushumai (an old man) and Nmi/Nmii (an old woman) representing ancestral spirits returning from the afterworld - bring flower-hatted descendants (faamaa) to invited homes, where they dance nenbutsu songs before the family altar and exchange humorous question-and-answer banter about the afterlife (Wikipedia, Angama (dance); Okinawa Clip). It is performed during the lunar-calendar Bon (sorin) in the 7th month.
angama.insight: Per Wikipedia, Angama shares its mainland Japanese (nenbutsu) origin with Okinawa's Eisa; nenbutsu practice was reportedly brought to Yaeyama in 1657 when the samurai leader Miyara Chouju traveled to Okinawa to pay tribute.

aati-kalenja.name: Aati Kalenja
aati-kalenja.tagline: Tulu monsoon-spirit dance that wards off disease
aati-kalenja.profile: Aati Kalenja is a ritual folk dance of Tulu Nadu (coastal Karnataka and Kasaragod, Kerala) performed during the Tulu month of Aati (July-August), the heavy-monsoon season (Wikipedia). A performer of the Nalike (or Mugera) community masquerades as the nature-spirit Kalenja, wearing a costume of tender coconut fronds and an areca-leaf headgear (mudi), face painted, holding a palm-leaf parasol. He visits homes dancing to the tembere drum while a companion sings the paddana, sprinkling water mixed with turmeric, charcoal and tamarind to drive away disease and misfortune (Swarajya; Daijiworld).
aati-kalenja.insight: The tradition is endangered: modernization and reduced paddy cultivation have left it confined to a few villages, prompting a Wikimedia-supported revival of the Mugera variant in 2024 (Wikimedia Diff).

cibi.name: Cibi
cibi.tagline: Fiji's Bauan war dance, the Flying Fijians' pre-match challenge
cibi.profile: The Cibi (pronounced 'thimbi') is a Fijian meke of Bauan origin, historically a war dance performed before or after battle (Wikipedia). On returning home victorious, warriors heralded their victory and were met by women singing with gestures. It came to prominence in 1939 when captain Ratu Sir George Cakobau, seeking an equivalent to the All Blacks' haka, approached Ratu Bola, high chief of the warrior clan of Navusaradave in Bau, who taught the team the Cibi; it has been the Fiji national rugby union team's pre-match ritual ever since (Wikipedia). It is also known as Teivovo after its opening chant 'Ai tei vovo'. In 2012 it was briefly replaced by the 'Bole' war cry before reverting.
cibi.insight: The Cibi is one of the Pacific's most recognizable sporting war dances, frequently and incorrectly conflated with the New Zealand haka; museum records (Alexander Turnbull Library) note historical photos 'previously incorrectly identified as a haka' (DigitalNZ).

video_stack.title: New Fijian war dance the "bole"

chozhikali.name: Chozhikali
chozhikali.tagline: Central Kerala masked harvest folk play of social satire
chozhikali.profile: Chozhikali (also Chozhi Kali / Chozikettu) is a folk dance of central Kerala, mainly the Valluvanad region of Palakkad and Thrissur districts, performed in two forms - Thiruvathirachozhi and Kudachozhi (also called Visharikali) (Wikipedia; Kerala Department of Cultural Affairs). Children dressed as the 'Chozhi' cover their bodies in dried banana and other leaves with masks of areca-palm petiole; the cast includes Yama, Chitragupta and the figure Muthi/Muthiyamma, enacting Yama's attempt to take Muthi to the afterlife (Wikipedia). Songs draw on the Ramayana and Mahabharata, accompanied by chenda and elathalam; Kudachozhi is performed by Pulaya-community families holding a palm-leaf umbrella and a bamboo stick as sword and shield (Wikipedia; Kerala Tourism).
chozhikali.insight: Chozhikali is now read as a subaltern art that satirically recreates the world of inequalities experienced during feudal times, with the umbrella and broom serving as symbols of power (Wikipedia).

babukung.name: Babukung
babukung.era: Traditional ritual; Babukung Festival staged since 2014
babukung.tagline: Masked Dayak Tomun funeral dance accompanying the soul
babukung.profile: Babukung is a funeral ritual masked dance of the Kaharingan religion practiced by the Dayak Tomun of Lamandau Regency, Central Kalimantan (Wikipedia). When a community member dies, masked dancers called Bukung come from neighboring villages wearing 'luha' masks representing animals and spirits to comfort the bereaved family, dispel evil spirits and honor the deceased's soul. The Babukung Festival has been officially recognized by the Lamandau Regency Government since 2014, using 15 mask categories including bird, dragon, crocodile, bat, hornbill, peacock, dog, butterfly and the white-faced 'sadap' mask (GuidepostTours).
babukung.insight: Wearing the luha mask symbolizes the dancer's transformation from human into spirit, bridging the living and the dead in Kaharingan belief (Indonesia.travel).

dainichido-bugaku.name: Dainichido Bugaku
dainichido-bugaku.tagline: Sacred New Year masked dances of Hachimantai, performed at dawn
dainichido-bugaku.profile: Dainichido Bugaku is a set of sacred ritual masked dances and music performed every 2 January from dawn to noon at Ohirumemuchi Shrine (commonly called Dainichido) in the Hachimantai district of Kazuno, Akita Prefecture, as a prayer for New Year happiness and good harvests (Wikipedia; UNESCO). According to legend, travelling bugaku performers of the imperial court visited in the early eighth century during the shrine's reconstruction and taught the dances to locals; the tradition is now transmitted by elders to the young within four communities - Osato, Azukisawa, Nagamine and Taniuchi - and includes masked dances (with the lion-like shishi) and child dancers. It was interrupted for nearly sixty years in the late 18th century before being revived.
dainichido-bugaku.insight: UNESCO inscribed Dainichido Bugaku on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2009; UNESCO notes the restored tradition is 'the spiritual core of [the community's] solidarity.'

buta-kola.name: Buta Kola
buta-kola.tagline: Tulu spirit-worship ritual of trance and possession
buta-kola.profile: Buta Kola (also Bhuta Kola, Daiva Nema) is a ritual spirit-worship and performance tradition of Tulu Nadu - Dakshina Kannada and Udupi in Karnataka and Kasaragod in Kerala (Wikipedia). A ritual specialist from communities such as the Nalike, Pambada or Parawa is possessed by a bhuta/daiva - spirit of a deified ancestor, hero or natural force - entering a trance to embody the deity in elaborate costume and body-painting, accompanied by music, recital of the spirit's origin-myth in Old Tulu, and dance. The kola honours a single spirit while the nema invokes several; both serve community functions of justice, protection and blessing (Wikipedia; The South First).
buta-kola.insight: Closely related to Kerala's Theyyam (regarded as its evolved form), Buta Kola gained wide attention after the 2022 film 'Kantara' depicted its elements, while the ritual remains a living marker of Tuluva identity (HandWiki; Mythlok).

devakkoothu.name: Devakkoothu
devakkoothu.era: Traditional (as old as the Chirakkal dynasty; revived 1985-86)
devakkoothu.tagline: The only Theyyam performed by a woman
devakkoothu.profile: Devakkoothu (also Devakoothu) is a ritual theyyam performed in Kerala at the Thekkumbad Koolom Thayakav temple near Cherukunnu in Kannur district - notable as the only theyyam performed by a woman (Wikipedia). The goddess embodied is Valliyamma, named for having become lost in a forest of creepers (valli); the performance narrates this myth, with Narada as a second character (Wikipedia). Only non-menstruating women may perform the role of Valliyamma, after a 41-day vrata, and the rite is held once every two years on the fifth day of the Malayalam month of Dhanu (December) (Wikipedia).
devakkoothu.insight: Believed to be as old as the Chirakkal dynasty, Devakkoothu lay dormant for many years and was revived in 1985-86; before 2012 it was performed for fourteen years by Lakshmi Amma, wife of Matai Kelu Panikar (Wikipedia).

gurdjieff-movements.name: Gurdjieff movements
gurdjieff-movements.tagline: Esoteric 'sacred dances' devised by G. I. Gurdjieff — NOT Chinese
gurdjieff-movements.profile: The Gurdjieff movements are a series of sacred dances created by mystic G. I. Gurdjieff (c.1866–1949) and taught to pupils to facilitate self-observation and self-study (English Wikipedia). Drawing on traditional dances Gurdjieff said he encountered in Central Asia, India, Tibet and among Sufi orders, the movements use precise, mathematically constructed postures and rhythms. Per English Wikipedia, 'Gurdjieff created and taught around fifty different movements between 1918 to when he died in Paris in 1949.'
gurdjieff-movements.insight: They represent a unique 20th-century attempt to treat dance as 'objective art' encoding esoteric knowledge, and remain central to Gurdjieffian 'Fourth Way' practice (English Wikipedia; Gurdjieff studies).

danza-de-los-voladores.name: Danza de los Voladores
danza-de-los-voladores.tagline: Mexico's UNESCO-listed pole flying ritual — four men descend headfirst from a 30-meter pole while a fifth plays flute on top.
danza-de-los-voladores.profile: The Danza de los Voladores (Spanish pronunciation: [ˈdansa ðe los βolaˈðoɾes]; "Dance of the Flyers"), or Palo Volador (pronounced [ˈpalo βolaˈðoɾ]; "flying pole"), is an ancient Mesoamerican ceremony/ritual still performed today, albeit in modified form, in isolated pockets in Mexico. It is believed to have originated with the Nahua, Huastec and Otomi peoples in central Mexico, and then spread throughout most of Mesoamerica.
danza-de-los-voladores.insight: == Intangible Cultural Heritage and conservation of the tradition == The Ritual Ceremony of the Voladores of Papantla was recognized as Intangible cultural heritage by UNESCO in 2009. The ceremony was named an Intangible cultural heritage by UNESCO in order to help the ritual survive and thrive in the modern world.

dhalo.name: Dhalo
dhalo.tagline: Goan women's nocturnal ritual dance of protection
dhalo.profile: Dhalo is a ritual folk dance of Goa performed exclusively by women as a prayer for the protection and prosperity of their households (Wikipedia). Conducted over roughly a week in the lunar month of Pausha at the onset of winter, 12-24 women dance in two parallel rows facing each other with interlocked arms, at a slower pace than the energetic Fugdi (Wikipedia). Songs are sung in Konkani or Marathi on religious and social themes and the dance is performed at a sacred open ground called the 'mand'; on the final day women dress elaborately and draw caricatures of men (Wikipedia; Gomantak Times).
dhalo.insight: Performed by Kunbi, Bhandari, Naik, Gabit and Gaudi communities, Dhalo functions as a living archive of Goan oral tradition - its 'oviyos' preserve folklore and devotional songs, traditionally said to descend from love songs Radha sang to Krishna (Wikipedia; ItsGoa).

eisa.name: Eisa
eisa.era: Origins in 17th-century nenbutsu Buddhist chant; modern competitive form developed in the 20th century
eisa.tagline: Okinawan ancestor-honoring drum dance of the Obon festival
eisa.profile: Eisa is a folk dance from Okinawa Island in the Ryukyu Islands, derived from the Obon dance performed by community youth to honor ancestral spirits (Wikipedia). Modern Eisa is danced by 20-30 young people in lines or circles, accompanied by singing and three drum types - the large odaiko, medium shimedaiko and small hand-held paarankuu - plus the three-stringed sanshin (Wikipedia). Its core consists of nembutsu songs such as Mamauya Ninbuchi; the 1713 Ryukyu-koku yuraiki attributes the introduction of nembutsu to the Jodo monk Taichu (1552-1639) (Wikipedia). The first Zento Eisa Contest was held in Koza in 1956, transforming Eisa into a spectacular group performance (Wikipedia).
eisa.insight: The 1956 Koza contest under U.S. occupation turned a solemn ancestral rite into competitive showmanship, and creative group Ryukyukoku Matsuri Daiko (formed 1982) spread Eisa internationally - operating, as of August 2024, 50 branches in Japan and 28 branches across eight other countries with roughly 2,500 members (Wikipedia; RMD Massachusetts).

dragon-dance.name: Dragon Dance
dragon-dance.tagline: A team-borne dragon undulating for luck and rain
dragon-dance.profile: The dragon dance (龍舞, longwu, also longdeng) is a traditional Chinese performance in which a team of dancers manipulates a long flexible dragon figure on poles (English Wikipedia). Tracing to the Han dynasty, it began as a ceremony to worship ancestors and pray for rain and later became festive entertainment, performed at Chinese New Year and Mid-Autumn Festival (Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art). The longer the dragon, the more luck it is said to bring.
dragon-dance.insight: Per English Wikipedia, 'The number of different dragon dances has been put at over 700,' making it among the most recognizable symbols of Chinese culture worldwide and a central New Year tradition.

dakkebali.name: Dakke Bali
dakkebali.tagline: Biennial Tulu serpent-worship ritual dance of Padubidri
dakkebali.profile: Dakke Bali is a form of Nagaradhane (serpent worship) practised by the Tulu people of Tulu Nadu, conducted chiefly at the Khadgeshwari Brahmasthana in Padubidri, Udupi district, Karnataka (Wikipedia; Mangalore Heritage). Held once every two years (in years when the Paryaya festival at Udupi does not occur), it runs on certain nights between roughly mid-January and mid-March (Wikipedia). A ritualist dressed as Nagakannika (the half-male/half-female serpent) plays the hourglass-shaped 'dakke' drum to invoke possession in the Patri/Pathri, who then moves in rhythmic circles around an elaborate serpent mandala drawn in natural colours, depicting the divine union of male and female snakes (Mangalore Heritage; The Sunday Guardian).
dakkebali.insight: Dakke Bali is, alongside Bhuta Kola, one of the principal ritual dance forms of Tulu Nadu; its nocturnal trance and serpent-mandala worship reflect the region's deep ecological and ancestral reverence for cobras, conducted strictly in lamplight without artificial lighting (Wikipedia; Mangalore Heritage).

diablada.name: Diablada
diablada.tagline: Bolivia's UNESCO-listed Devil Dance — Oruro Carnival's Lucifer faces off against the Archangel Michael, masked dancers in flames descending the Andean streets.
diablada.profile: The Diablada, also known as the Danza de los Diablos (English: Dance of the Devils), is an Andean folk dance performed in Bolivia, in the Altiplano region of South America, characterized by performers wearing masks and costumes representing the devil and other characters from pre-Columbian theology and mythology. combined with Spanish and Christian elements added during the colonial era.
diablada.insight: The first institutionalized Diablada dance squad was the Gran Tradicional y Auténtica Diablada Oruro, founded in Bolivia in 1904 by Pedro Pablo Corrales.
sources: Source: Diablada on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diablada

gadhika.name: Gadhika
gadhika.tagline: Adiya healing ritual to appease angry gods
gadhika.profile: Gadhika (also Gaddika) is a ritual art of the Adiya (Adiyor) scheduled-tribe community of Wayanad district, Kerala, performed to cure disease and ward off misfortune and the evil eye (Wikipedia; Kerala Tourism). The tribe believes that sickness arises from divine displeasure, so the chief priest (Gaddikakaran/Moopan), dressed in red, invokes Lord Shiva, after which deities such as Chamundi, Maniamma, Malamkali and Karimkali are believed to arrive (Kerala Tourism). The dialect blends Kannada and Tulu; it has two forms - public Naattu Gadhika and ritualistic Pooja Gadhika (the latter performed to cure illness or for the safe delivery of a child) - accompanied by wind instruments and drums, often in the Malayalam month of Mithunam (June-July) (Wikipedia; Kerala Tourism).
gadhika.insight: Under the leadership of the Adiya Mooppan and politician P. K. Kalan, Gadhika - once purely ritual - was brought to public platforms inside and outside Kerala without losing its artistic values, and the Kerala Scheduled Tribes Development Department's tribal art fair is named 'Gadhika' in its honour (Wikipedia).

acharuli.name: Acharuli
acharuli.tagline: Adjara's bright, flirtatious Black Sea coastal dance
acharuli.profile: Acharuli is a bright, cheerful dance originating in Adjara on Georgia's Black Sea coast, portraying playful, informal flirtation between men and women - unlike the strict Kartuli, the male-female interaction is relaxed and almost frivolous (Wikipedia; Georgian National Ballet Sukhishvili). Dancers wear colorful costumes predominantly featuring red; the choreographic suite is built on the Adjarian folk dance and song Gandagana. It alternates slow and fast movements accompanied by polyphonic music and instruments such as the bagpipe (chiboni), panduri, doli and accordion.
acharuli.insight: Acharuli reflects the distinct culture of Adjara, a region under Ottoman influence from roughly the 16th to mid-19th centuries, and its Gandagana basis is a recognized Monument of Intangible Cultural Heritage of Georgia (Georgia Today).

ai-georgis.name: Ai Georgis
ai-georgis.tagline: A processional dance from the village of Nestani, Arkadia, performed on St. George’s feast day.
ai-georgis.profile: Ai Georgis is a traditional dance originating from the village of Nestani in the Arkadia region of the Peloponnesus, Greece. Performed annually on the feast day of St. George, typically following Easter Sunday, the dance serves as a communal commemoration of historical protection. The performance is characterized by a gendered procession where men lead the line, carrying shepherd's crooks decorated with greenery and wildflowers. The dance is accompanied exclusively by song, featuring complex rhythmic structures in 7/8 and 2/4 time. It is a living tradition that integrates local history and religious observance into a structured movement sequence.
ai-georgis.insight: On the feast of St. George in Nestani, men lead a line of dancers while holding shepherd’s crooks entwined with fresh wildflowers and green leaves to commemorate protection from the Ottomans.
sources: Source: Ai Georgis on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ai_Georgis
ai-georgis.profile_long: The dance of Ai Georgis is deeply rooted in the village identity of Nestani, located in the Arkadia region of the Peloponnesus. The region itself derives its name from the mythological figure Arcas, grounding the dance in a landscape of ancient significance. The performance is intrinsically linked to the feast day of St. George, occurring in the period immediately following Easter Sunday. This timing aligns the dance with the spring season, a period reflected in the physical props used by the participants. The men, who lead the dance, carry shepherd's crooks that have been carefully entwined with fresh green leaves and wildflowers. This visual motif of the crook serves as a symbol of the pastoral life of the region and the specific historical narrative of the dance. The lyrics accompanying the dance are not merely rhythmic markers; they recount the protection of the villagers from the Ottomans and reference the Hagia Sophia, connecting the local experience of Nestani to broader historical and religious themes. The structure of the dance is precise, consisting of ten basic steps organized into four distinct parts. The movement is led by men, with women following in the line, creating a gendered formation that moves through the village space. The musical accompaniment is strictly vocal, relying on the power of song to drive the movement. The rhythm is notably complex, utilizing both 7/8 and 2/4 time signatures, which dictates the cadence of the dancers' steps. The dance is a living tradition, maintained by the community of Nestani as a way to honor their history and their patron saint. Because the dance is performed on a religious feast day, it carries a specific cultural weight, serving as both a social gathering and a ritual act. The reliance on the shepherd's crook as a primary prop distinguishes it from other Greek folk dances, emphasizing the connection between the dance and the agricultural and pastoral heritage of the Arkadian people. The transition between the 7/8 and 2/4 rhythms requires a high degree of coordination among the dancers, who must maintain the line while navigating the ten-step sequence. The dance remains a focal point of the village's annual calendar, preserving the memory of the struggles and the faith of the community through the medium of song and movement.
ai-georgis.sacred_note: The dance is performed on a religious feast day (St. George) and involves specific ritual props (crooks) and themes of historical protection.

abay.name: Abayı
abay.era: Traditional; melody composed by Shaki composers
abay.tagline: Shaki's comic dance poking fun at middle age
abay.profile: Abayı (Azerbaijani: Abayı) is an Azerbaijani folk dance originating in the Shaki and Zaqatala regions, whose subject is middle age — in this area middle-aged people are called "Abayı" — and which is performed with slightly exaggerated, comic movements at a slow tempo (Wikipedia; Azerbaijani dances). Its melody was written by Shaki composers; once a group dance, it later evolved into a solo form, traditionally accompanied by instruments such as the tar, kamancha, saz and daf.
abay.insight: Abayı is a rare example of gently satirical folk dance: by exaggerating the gestures of the middle-aged, it turns the dignity of age into affectionate comedy, reflecting the regional humor of the Shaki–Zaqatala area (Wikipedia).

acro-dance.name: Acro dance
acro-dance.tagline: A fusion of classical dance technique and precision acrobatic elements.
acro-dance.profile: Acro dance is a performance style that integrates classical dance foundations—such as ballet, jazz, and contemporary—with athletic acrobatic 'tricks.' Unlike gymnastics, which prioritizes sport-governed scoring, acro dance emphasizes fluid, graceful transitions between dance and movement. It is a prominent feature in contemporary circus, competitive dance, and professional theater.
acro-dance.insight: Sherman Coates (1872–1912), who performed with the Watermelon Trust from 1900 to 1914, was recalled by fellow dancers as the first acrobatic dancer they had ever seen.
sources: Source: Acro dance on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acro_dance

_albums.title: Acrobatic Dance: Music from the Gulag

acro-dance.profile_long: Acro dance, often referred to simply as 'acro,' is a style of dance that combines classical dance technique with acrobatic elements. It is defined by its athletic character, its unique choreography, which blends dance and acrobatics, and its use of acrobatics in a dance context. It is a popular dance style in amateur competitive dance as well as in professional dance theater and in contemporary circus productions such as those by Cirque du Soleil. This is in contrast to acrobatic, artistic and rhythmic gymnastics, which are sports that employ dance elements in a gymnastics context under the auspices of a governing gymnastics organization (such as FIG) and subject to a Code of Points. Acro dance is known by various other names including acrobatic dance and gymnastic dance. Acro is an especially challenging dance style for dancers as it requires them to be trained in both dance and acrobatic skills. Acrobatic dance emerged in the United States and Canada in the early 1900s, as one of the types of acts performed in vaudeville. Although individual dance and acrobatic acts had been performed in vaudeville for several decades prior to 1900, it was not until the early 1900s that it became popular to perform acts that combined dance and acrobatic movements. Acrobatic dance did not suddenly appear in vaudeville; rather, it appeared gradually over time in a variety of forms, and consequently no individual performer has been cited as its originator. Sherman Coates (1872–1912), who performed with the Watermelon Trust from 1900 to 1914, was recalled by fellow dancers as the first acrobatic dancer they had ever seen. Another of the earliest documented acrobatic dance performers was Tommy Woods, who became well known for his slow-motion acrobatic dance in Shuffle Along, in which he would execute acrobatic movements precisely in time with the music. In 1914, acrobat Lulu Coates formed the Crackerjacks, a popular vaudeville troupe that included acrobatic dance in their performance repertoire up until the group disbanded in 1952. Many other popular vaudeville companies combined acrobatics and dance in their shows, including the Gaines Brothers, and Miriam (The acrobatic Tapper) who performed with the Wells & The Four Fays 'Tumbling Acrobats' on The Ed Sullivan Show on February 9, 1964. Since the decline of the vaudeville era, acrobatic dance has undergone a multi-faceted evolution to arrive at its present-day form. The most significant aspect of this evolution is the integration of ballet technique as the foundation for dance movements, thus bringing into acro dance a precision of form and movement that was absent in vaudeville acrobatic dance. Also, vaudeville acrobatic dances were often little more than acrobatics set to music, whereas modern acro dance is fundamentally dance, with its acrobatic movements performed in a dance context. A defining characteristic of acro is the smooth, graceful transitions between dance and acrobatic movements. Also, a dance must have a significant percentage of dance movement, with respect to its acrobatic content, in order for it to be categorized as acro. For example, a gymnastics floor exercise is not considered to be Acro Dance because it has little or no technical dance movement, compared to its acrobatic content. It also lacks smooth transitions between dance and gymnastic movements. Also, Acro Dance does not employ supporting apparatus such as those used in acrobatic gymnastics. The dance movements in Acro Dance are founded in ballet, jazz, lyrical, contemporary and modern dance styles. Acro dance movements are not restricted to these dance styles, but the complete absence of these styles will typically cause a dance to be categorized as something other than acro (e.g., breakdance). The acrobatic movements and acts of balance performed in an acro dance are referred to as tricks. A variety of tricks are commonly performed in acro dance, varying widely in complexity and the skills required to perform them. Aside from the obvious requirement that dancers possess the requisite skills to perform tricks, the types of tricks that can be performed in an acro dance depends on the number of dancers. Strength, flexibility and balance are also major pillars of Acro Dance, and postures often inspired by those of contortion are used throughout Acro Dance along side agility (tricks) and dance technique. Acro dancers commonly wear flexible, form-fitting clothing for both safety and aesthetic reasons. Form-fitting clothing is preferred over loose clothing because the latter does not move synchronously with the body and thus may interfere with a dancer's ability to maintain control. This is especially important when a dancer is performing tricks, as loss of control can lead to serious injury. Aside from the safety aspect, form-fitting clothing also helps to expose a dancer's body lines, which can add significantly to the visual impact of an acro dance performance.

agir-karadagi.name: Agir Karadagi
agir-karadagi.tagline: A slow, heavy dance-melody from Karadakh
agir-karadagi.profile: Agir Karadagi (Azerbaijani: Ağır Qaradağı, meaning "heavy Karadakhi") is an Azerbaijani dance song that originated in the historic region of Karadakh and is very popular in the Shaki and Zaqatala regions, performed slowly (Azerbaijani dances, Wikipedia). As with much Azerbaijani folk dance, it follows the genre's smooth-to-lively character and is accompanied by traditional instruments; the musical meter of Azerbaijani dances is typically 6/8 or 3/4.
agir-karadagi.insight: Agir Karadagi exemplifies the many Azerbaijani dances named for their place of origin (Karadakh) and tempo ("heavy"/slow), part of a folk repertoire whose antiquity is evidenced by the prehistoric rock carvings at Gobustan (Azernews).

abbots-bromley-horn-dance.name: Abbots Bromley Horn Dance
abbots-bromley-horn-dance.tagline: United Kingdom — folk dance which takes place each September in the village of Abbots Bromley in Staffordshire, England
abbots-bromley-horn-dance.profile: The Abbots Bromley Horn Dance is a folk dance which takes place each September in the village of Abbots Bromley in Staffordshire, England. It is performed by ten dancers, accompanied by a musician playing an accordion and a youth with a triangle. Six of the dancers carry reindeer horns; the remaining four take the roles of a hobby horse, Maid Marian, a fool, and a youth with a bow and arrow. On Wakes Monday the performers dance around the parish all day, beginning early in the morning at the parish church where the horns are stored. The origin of the dance is unknown.
abbots-bromley-horn-dance.insight: The earliest written record of a hobby-horse performance at Abbots Bromley dates to 1532, and the first mention of the reindeer horns is from 1686.

agwara.profile: Agwara is a royal dance of the Alur people of Northern Uganda and parts of the WestNile sub-region, performed in the presence of the king (Rwot). It is performed by both women and men during social occasions. The dance is performed to drums, and uses linear and circular formations characterized by leg and waist twisting while wearing ankle bells to emphasize their footwork. The dance is named after the sound of long trumpets also known as agwara horns.
agwara.insight: Agwara is a royal dance of the Alur people of Northern Uganda and parts of the WestNile sub-region, performed in the presence of the king (Rwot).
