aparima.name: Aparima
aparima.profile: The aparima (apa 'movement/mimic' + rima 'hands') is a gesture dance from Tahiti and the Cook Islands in which the hands narrate a story, close in spirit to hula and the Tongan tauolunga. Two types exist: aparima vava (mute pantomime, often kneeling, accompanied by pahu and toere) and aparima himene (sung, with stringed instruments such as guitar/ukulele). Costuming is a pareu or cloth dress; gestures are descriptive, symbolic or ornamental (English Wikipedia; Tahiti dance online).
aparima.insight: Unlike the oteea, the aparima is soft and narrative - the only Tahitian form always meant to pantomime an actual story (Tahiti dance online).

allemande.name: Allemande
allemande.tagline: The Renaissance partner dance from German lands — stately processional that became Bach's Baroque opener.
allemande.profile: An allemande (French pronunciation: [almɑ̃d] , "German (dance)"; also allemanda, almain(e), or alman(d)) is a Renaissance and Baroque dance, and one of the most common instrumental dance styles in Baroque music, with examples by Couperin, Purcell, Bach and Handel. It is often the first movement of a Baroque suite of dances, paired with a subsequent courante, though it is sometimes preceded by an introduction or prelude. Along with the waltz and ländler, the allemande was sometimes referred to by the generic term German Dance in publications during the late 18th and early 19th centuries.
allemande.insight: The allemande became the standard opening movement of the Baroque dance suite — J.S. Bach wrote dozens of them across his partitas, English Suites, and French Suites, and Handel, Couperin, and Telemann followed suit. While its dance practice faded by the 18th century, its musical form became one of the foundations of Western classical structure; today historical-dance ensembles in London, Paris, and Boston perform reconstructed allemandes from period sources.

an-dro.name: An Dro
an-dro.era: Traditional; revived from the 1950s in fest-noz
an-dro.tagline: Breton round/chain dance from the Vannetais, pinky-linked.
an-dro.profile: An dro (Breton 'the turn') is a Breton folk dance in 4/4, a form of circle/chain dance originating in the pays Vannetais of southern Lower Brittany (Wikipedia). Dancers form a long open line (or couples in cortege, then called kas a-barh), joined by hooking their little fingers and swinging the arms; the step takes a short move right and a longer move left so the chain drifts steadily leftward, the leader at the left end drawing spirals. An dro is considered an 'arm dance' (vs. the 'feet dances' gavotte/hanter-dro). It is sung (call-and-response) or played on biniou/bombarde, accordion and other fest-noz instruments. An dro tunes are central to the Breton repertoire from Alan Stivell and Tri Yann to the rock band Matmatah.
an-dro.insight: One of the most widely known Breton dances outside Brittany, performed within the UNESCO-inscribed fest-noz tradition (Wikipedia; UNESCO).

angelica.tagline: Greece — The Angelica or Angelike (Greek: Ἀγγελική) was a celebrated dance among the ancient Greeks, performed at their
angelica.profile: The Angelica or Angelike (Greek: Ἀγγελική) was a celebrated dance among the ancient Greeks, performed at their feasts and important celebrations. It was thus called from the Greek ἄγγελος (angelos, "messenger"), by reason, as Pollux assures us, the dancers were dressed in the habit of messengers. This dance was perfected by the Syracusans and performed at their drinking parties. It is probably the same as the messenger's dance, called the Angelikon, which involved a series of gestures to the audience to illustrate the messenger's account of events that occurred off-stage during certain plays.

alkayida.tagline: Ghanaian Azonto-era street dance popularised by hiplife artist Guru
alkayida.profile: Alkayida (also spelt Akayida) is a Ghanaian street dance emphasizing side-to-side moves, upper-body gestures and footwork-heavy freestyling, encouraging group routines and individual competition (Wikipedia). It emerged from Accra youth styling around 2013 and was popularised by hiplife artist Guru's song 'Akayida (Boys Abre)' (Wikipedia; Red Bull). The name controversially echoes 'Al-Qaeda'; Guru and other proponents insist on the spelling 'Akayida' and disavow any link to the terrorist organization, with the parenthetical 'Boys Abre' meaning 'boys are tired' (Wikipedia; Grandmother Africa).
alkayida.insight: Afropop Worldwide noted that Alkayida tunes are markedly slower than Azonto with a pronounced one-two swing, distinguishing it from the earlier craze it was initially dismissed as an offshoot of (Afropop Worldwide).

argentine-tango.name: Argentine Tango
argentine-tango.tagline: Close-embrace improvised partner dance of Río de la Plata passion.
argentine-tango.profile: Argentine tango is a partner dance and musical genre that developed in the working-class immigrant neighborhoods (arrabales) and academias of Buenos Aires and Montevideo in the late 19th century, evolving from milonga, candombe, and habanera. It is danced in a close or open embrace built on improvised walking, with the bandoneón giving the orquesta típica its distinctive voice (English Wikipedia). Lyrics are marked by nostalgia and lost love; leading figures include Carlos Gardel and Ástor Piazzolla.
argentine-tango.insight: Tango was recognized by Argentina's Ley 24.684 (1996) as integral to the nation's cultural patrimony, covering its music, lyrics, and dance; it embodies and encourages cultural dialogue across the Río de la Plata (Argentina InfoLeg; UNESCO).

asma-kasma.name: Asma kasma
asma-kasma.era: One of the oldest Azerbaijani dances
asma-kasma.tagline: A slow, leaping wedding dance escorting the bride
asma-kasma.profile: Asma Kasma (Azerbaijani: Asma Kəsmə, "hanging cutting") is described as one of the oldest Azerbaijani dances, performed at weddings: it accompanies the escorting of the bride to the bridegroom's home, with women dancing opposite the bride. Its tempo is slow and slightly exaggerated and the dance is full of jumps (Azerbaijani dances / en-academic; AzerNews). It takes its name from the music called "Asma-Kasma."
asma-kasma.insight: As a dedicated bridal-procession dance, asma kasma is part of the ceremonial (wedding) category of Azerbaijani folk dance, marking the bride's transition between households in a tradition reaching back to the early Middle Ages (Azerbaijani dances).

ardah.name: Ardah
ardah.tagline: type of folkloric group dance in the Arabian Peninsula, in most countries located in the Gulf Cooperation Coun
ardah.profile: Ardah (Arabic: العرضة / ALA-LC: al-‘arḍah) is a type of folkloric group dance in the Arabian Peninsula, in most countries located in the Gulf Cooperation Council. The dance is performed with two rows of men opposite of one another, each of whom may or may not be wielding a sword or cane, and is accompanied by drums and spoken poetry. Originally, the ardah was performed only by males of tribes of the Arabian Peninsula before going to war, but nowadays it is done at celebrations, weddings, and national and cultural events by males of all tribes.
ardah.insight: It was inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2015 as Alardah Alnajdiyah.

atilogwu.name: Atilogwu
atilogwu.tagline: Nigeria — spirited youth dance from the Igbo ethnic group of Nigeria that focuses on vigorous body movement and often in
atilogwu.profile: Atilogwu is a spirited youth dance from the Igbo ethnic group of Nigeria that focuses on vigorous body movement and often includes acrobatics. In the Igbo language, the word itself "Atilogwu" translates into "has magic, as in sorcery/witchcraft". The name stems from rumors that bewitchment or magic potions had to be involved if the children of the village could perform so exuberantly and energetically, while making it look so effortless. The tempo of the dance matches the tempo of the music, which is dependent on the beat of the drum and ogene, a metal gong instrument.
atilogwu.insight: Atilogwu is a spirited youth dance from the Igbo ethnic group of Nigeria that focuses on vigorous body movement and often includes acrobatics.

azonto.name: Azonto

azonto.profile: Azonto is a dance and music genre from Ghana connected to the traditional Ga dance Kpanlogo, associated with coastal Greater Accra towns such as Chorkor, James Town, Teshie, Nungua and Tema (Wikipedia). Several accounts say it was formerly known as 'Apaa' ('work'); its hand movements mimic everyday activities (washing, driving, ironing, praying). One foot is planted while the other pivots on the ball; the hands trace flowing circular motions (Wikipedia). Per Red Bull, following Sarkodie and E.L.'s 2011 'U Go Kill Me', the Azonto craze rapidly took over Ghana and African diaspora communities in the UK and US.
azonto.insight: Popular-music researcher Jesse Weaver Shipley argues that, like hiplife, Azonto's popularity stems from diaspora interactions - identified with Ghanaian indigeneity by those abroad and with cosmopolitanism by those at home (Wikipedia).

awki-awki.name: Awki awki
awki-awki.tagline: A Bolivian-Peruvian folk dance satirizing elderly Spanish colonial conquerors.
awki-awki.profile: Awki awki is a folk dance performed in the La Paz Department of Bolivia and the Huancané Province of Peru. Derived from the Aymara word auqui, meaning father or old man with a reduplication indicating a collective noun, the dance satirizes elderly Spanish conquerors of the colonial period. Performers wear formal colonial suits, large woven straw hats, and masks with long white beards.
awki-awki.insight: In Awki awki, men don masks with long white beards and large woven straw hats to satirize the elderly Spanish conquerors of the colonial period.
sources: Source: Awki awki on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Awki_awki
awki-awki.profile_long: Awki awki, also known as Auqui Auqui, is a traditional folk dance documented in the La Paz Department of Bolivia and the Huancané Province of Peru. The name originates from the Aymara word auqui, which translates to father or old man. The term features a reduplication that forms a collective noun, indicating a group of such figures. Culturally and historically, the dance serves as a form of satire directed at the elderly Spanish conquerors of the colonial period. In terms of performance and attire, the dance is executed exclusively by men. Participants wear distinct costumes that represent formal colonial-era suits. Their physical presentation is enhanced by large hats made of woven straw and detailed masks that depict elderly men characterized by long white beards. Beyond these core descriptive elements derived from foundational records, detailed accounts regarding specific choreography, musical accompaniment, footwork patterns, instrumentation, and performance occasions remain largely unrecorded in current documentation.

atsiapat.profile: Atsiapat (Pontic: Άτσιαπατ), also spelt atsapat (Άτσαπατ), is the first in a sequence of three Pontic Greek male dances performed in the region of Pontus, as well as by refugees of Pontos. Atsapat is the Greek pronunciation of the Pontic Turkish city of Akçaabat. The region is famous for the virtuosity of its Pyrrhichios dancers.

attan.name: Attan
attan.era: Ancient; possible Zoroastrian/pre-Islamic roots, codified over centuries
attan.tagline: Afghanistan's whirling circle dance, drum-driven and proudly national
attan.profile: Attan is the national dance of Afghanistan, originating among Pashtun tribes of southern and eastern Afghanistan and northwestern Pakistan. Dancers form a circle around a dohol (double-headed barrel drum) player, beginning with slow steps that accelerate, with spins, hand-claps, head and hair flicks, and handkerchiefs; a performance can last 5 to 30 minutes (Wikipedia; Britannica). Once danced by warriors before battle, it now features at weddings, engagements and Nowruz; regional styles include Kabuli, Logari, Paktia/Khosti, Wardaki, Kandahari and Herati.
attan.insight: Britannica notes the open-air Attan "became the national dance of the Pashtun and then of the entire country," and it was banned under the Taliban; Afghanistan has applied to UNESCO to register it (Arab News), making it a potent emblem of Afghan identity, though it has not yet been inscribed.

bagurumba.name: Bagurumba
bagurumba.tagline: The Bodo 'butterfly dance' mirroring nature's grace
bagurumba.profile: Bagurumba is a traditional dance of the indigenous Bodo (Boro) people of Assam, nicknamed the 'butterfly dance' because its slow, poised movements imitate butterflies, birds and swaying flowers (Wikipedia). Performed mainly by women during the spring festival Bwishagu (mid-April), dancers wear the colourful handwoven dokhona, jwmgra (fasra) and aronai, using the jwmgra cloth like butterfly wings. It is accompanied by instruments including the sifung (long bamboo flute), serja (bowed instrument), kham (drum), jota and gongwna (Wikipedia; The Better India).

asyik.name: Asyik
asyik.tagline: Classical royal court dance created in 1644 to comfort a grieving queen.
asyik.profile: Asyik is a classical royal court dance popular in Patani and Kelantan. According to the Hikayat Patani, it originated in 1644 for the grieving Ratu Kuning. Ten dancers begin seated before the prima donna, Puteri Asyik, performs delicate gestures. The tradition later spread to common folk for weddings and festivals.
asyik.insight: In 1644, the classical court dance Asyik was created to console Queen Ratu Kuning over the loss of her favorite bird.
sources: Source: Asyik on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asyik
asyik.profile_long: Asyik (literally meaning "beloved" or "besotted") is a classical royal court dance popular in Patani and Kelantan. According to the Hikayat Patani, the dance was created in 1644 to entertain the grieving Ratu Kuning over the loss of her favorite bird, and its name may refer to that lost bird. The performance begins with ten beautifully costumed dancers entering the dancing hall and sitting gracefully. Following their entrance, the prima donna, also known as Puteri Asyik ("the princess of love"), appears to begin the dance with gracious and delicate body movements and gestures. The musical accompaniment is provided by an orchestra consisting of gedombak asyik (a small drum), gambang (a xylophone-like instrument, usually made of slabs of wood or bronze), and a rebab (a bowed lute). Although it began strictly as a court dance, over time the dance became popular among common people and was used as folk entertainment during festivals and marriages.

balboa.name: Balboa
balboa.tagline: Balboa Peninsula, California, 1932 — the dance invented because kicks and aerials were banned. Crowded ballroom Lindy in chest-to-chest hold.
balboa.profile: The Balboa, also known as "Bal", is a swing dance that emerged in Southern California during the early 1930s as a response to swing music. The earliest recorded reference to Balboa is 1932. This date coincides with what is generally accepted to be the beginning of swing. The dance enjoyed huge popularity in California during the 1930s and 1940s, and was still being danced by original dancers into the 21st century. Balboa is a social partner dance that distinctively relies on closed position. The earliest form of the dance emerged in the high schools and dance venues of southern California.
balboa.insight: It was created for the Panama Californian Exhibition, Balboa Park, 1915-17, with illustrated instructions published in newspapers.

baile-de-la-conquista.tagline: Spain — traditional folkloric dance from Guatemala
baile-de-la-conquista.profile: The Baile de la Conquista or Dance of the Conquest is a traditional folkloric dance from Guatemala. The dance reenacts the invasion led by Spanish conquistador Pedro de Alvarado and his confrontation with Tecun Uman, ruler of K'iche' kingdom of Q'umarkaj. Although the dance is more closely associated with Guatemalan traditions, it has been performed in early colonial regions of Latin America at the urging of Catholic friars and priests, as a method of converting various native populations and African slaves to the Catholic Church.

bajidor-kahot.name: Bajidor Kahot
bajidor-kahot.tagline: Modern Sundanese dance fusing Ketuk Tilu and Jaipongan
bajidor-kahot.profile: Bajidor Kahot is a modern Sundanese created group dance from West Java which combines the dance movements of Ketuk Tilu and Jaipongan as the basis of its motions (Wikipedia). It was created around the year 2000 and is typically performed by young women in brightly colored Sundanese kebaya using fans (kipas) and scarves (selendang), shifting through dynamic formations. The dance is accompanied by Sundanese kendang drumming and gamelan, and its roots trace to the older Kliningan-Bajidoran folk performance of the Karawang and Subang regions.
bajidor-kahot.insight: As an 'invented tradition,' Bajidor Kahot exemplifies how late-20th-century choreographers repackaged Sundanese folk vocabulary into accessible stage repertoire (Budaya-Indonesia).

baishou-dance.name: Baishou Dance
baishou-dance.profile: The Baishou Dance (摆手舞, baishouwu, 'hand-waving dance') is a group ritual dance of the Tujia people of Xiangxi, Hunan. Per English Wikipedia, 'It originates from an ancestor worship ceremony and dates back nearly 1,000 years ago, according to the broken stele in the Temple of Eight Clan Leaders (Qing Dynasty) and the county annals.' It uses 70 ritual gestures to represent war, farming, hunting, courtship and other aspects of traditional life, accompanied by gongs and drums. Per the Department of Culture and Tourism of Hunan Province, 'Grand Baishou is performed by over 1,000 dancers when offering sacrifices to the ancestors of the whole group.'
baishou-dance.insight: It is one of China's oldest continuous folk dances and a key carrier of Tujia history, recognized as national intangible cultural heritage (Hunan provincial government).

ball-dels-cossiers.name: Ball dels Cossiers
ball-dels-cossiers.tagline: Majorcan folk dance where six dancers and a Lady defend good against a demon.
ball-dels-cossiers.profile: The Ball dels Cossiers is the most popular traditional dance on the island of Majorca in the Spanish Balearic Islands. The performance features six dancers typically arranged in three pairs who defend a figure representing good, known as the Lady, from a demon. Brought to the island from Catalonia following the 14th-century Aragonian conquest, the dance nearly vanished under 20th-century political repression before a 1962 revival. Today, it is practiced exclusively in Palma and five surrounding towns.
ball-dels-cossiers.insight: In 1962, film director José María Oliveira revived the banned Ball dels Cossiers at his hotel in Palma after decades of Franco's cultural repression.
sources: Source: Ball dels Cossiers on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ball_dels_Cossiers
ball-dels-cossiers.profile_long:
Origins and History: The Ball dels Cossiers traces its recorded presence on Majorca back to the 14th century, arriving from Catalonia following the Aragonian conquest under King Jaime I. The earliest documented evidence of the dance appears in a 1544 manuscript originating in Sóller. Scholars debate its deeper roots, with some arguing the tradition stems from ancient pagan nature spirit worshipping rituals native to the island, subsequently fusing with incoming Catalan customs and Corpus Christi processions. During the 20th century, the dance all but disappeared due to Francisco Franco's strict repression of Majorcan and Catalan culture. The turning point arrived in 1962 when Spanish film director José María Oliveira initiated performances at his hotel in Palma, rallying local troupes to resurrect the tradition.

How It Is Danced: The performance features six dancers—known as cossiers, though the precise number can vary—alongside a central figure called the Lady, who may be portrayed by either a man or a woman. In many locations, a demon character interacts with the group. Normally, the dance is executed in a circle with the Lady positioned directly in the center. However, certain solemn traditional troupes—specifically named as La Oferta, els Mocadors, the Bandanas, and the Mercançó—deviate from this standard circular formation.

Music and Instruments: Specific musical scores, instrumental configurations, and rhythmic meters are not described in sources.

Costume and Setting: Specific costume designs, textiles, and performance settings beyond public festivals and fiestas are not described in sources.

Occasions and Meaning: The dance is performed during festivals, fiestas, and public events, historically linking to Corpus Christi processions and seasonal celebrations where dancers symbolically defend goodness represented by the Lady against the disruptive presence of a demon.

Notable Figures: Spanish film director José María Oliveira stands out as a pivotal figure who catalyzed the modern revival of the dance in 1962 by hosting performances at his Palma hotel and supporting local troupes.

Regional Variants: While once widespread across the island, the contemporary practice of the Ball dels Cossiers is restricted to Palma and five specific towns and villages on Majorca: Manacor, Alaró, Algaida, Montuïri, and Inca. Particular troupes such as La Oferta, els Mocadors, the Bandanas, and the Mercançó maintain distinct, more solemn spatial formations that depart from the standard circle.

Lineage: The dance operates as a subclass of Catalan folk dance, originating via Catalan repopulators and settlers during the medieval era.

ballos.name: Ballos
ballos.tagline: A Greek island courtship dance characterized by flirtation and lyrical melodies.
ballos.profile: The Ballos is a traditional Greek couples' dance deeply rooted in the island culture of the Aegean. It functions as a choreographed courtship ritual, incorporating themes of attraction, pursuit, and eventual surrender. While it manifests in various forms across the islands, it is fundamentally a social dance that allows for both individual expression and collective participation.
ballos.insight: On the Greek islands, the Ballos emerged as a courtship ritual where men, unable to approach women directly, used the dance to display prowess and pursue partners through a series of flirtatious figures.
sources: Source: Ballos on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballos
ballos.profile_long: The Ballos is a quintessential expression of Greek island culture, serving as a structured medium for courtship and social interaction. Its name is etymologically linked to the Greek verb 'ballizo', meaning 'to dance' or 'to jump', tracing a path through the Latin and Italian 'ballo'. Historically, the dance emerged from the social constraints of island life, where direct interaction between men and women was limited. The Ballos provided a culturally sanctioned space for men to approach women, allowing for the display of masculine prowess and the demonstration of feminine virtue through a series of stylized movements. The dance is inherently a couples' performance, though its execution varies significantly across different regions. In its simplest form, a single couple performs a sequence of spontaneous figures, while in more complex iterations, multiple couples may dance simultaneously, creating an atmosphere of shared social engagement. Some versions of the Ballos are introduced by a Sirtos, a common Greek dance form, while others incorporate intricate figures that have been compared to the European minuet. The emotional tone of the dance is highly dependent on the regional context. In the Aegean islands, the music is typically joyous and lyrical, reflecting the vibrant character of the local island music. In contrast, the Cypriot variant of the Ballos is distinct; it is performed primarily by men and is deeply interwoven with 'amane' type songs, which are based on the Byzantine scale. These Cypriot songs are characterized by their melancholy and require a highly skilled vocalist to execute properly. The dance serves as a narrative of courtship, moving through distinct phases of attraction, flirtation, pursuit, and rejection, before culminating in a symbolic capture and surrender. This progression is not merely a sequence of steps but a social performance that reflects the values and interpersonal dynamics of the community. Because the dance is so deeply embedded in the social fabric of the islands, it remains a popular tradition with a vast repertoire of songs. The Ballos continues to be a living tradition, maintained by the communities that value its role in preserving the history of island courtship and the lyrical heritage of the Aegean and beyond. Whether performed as a simple, spontaneous interaction or a complex, multi-couple display, the Ballos remains a vital link to the historical and cultural identity of the Greek islands.

bamboula.name: Bamboula
bamboula.tagline: A West African-derived drum and syncopated dance tradition of the Caribbean and Louisiana.
bamboula.profile: The bamboula is both a percussion instrument—a cylindrical friction drum—and a syncopated dance tradition originating from West African cultures. Exported to the Caribbean and the United States, it became a focal point of communal gatherings in New Orleans' Congo Square during the 19th century. The tradition is deeply intertwined with the history of the African diaspora, though the term has also been historically appropriated as a racial slur in French-speaking regions.
bamboula.insight: In 1757, the bamboula appeared in a Haitian song, later becoming a central, syncopated dance in New Orleans' Congo Square before the term was repurposed as an ethnic slur in 19th-century French colonial discourse.
sources: Source: Bamboula on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bamboula
bamboula.profile_long:
The bamboula represents a complex intersection of musical, social, and linguistic history. Originating from West African traditions, specifically those of the Fon, Yoruba, Serer, and Jola-Fonyi peoples, the term itself is derived from words meaning 'drum' in languages spoken in Portuguese Guinea. As an instrument, the bamboula is a cylindrical friction drum, often constructed from a rum barrel with skin stretched over one or both ends. It stands approximately one meter high with a diameter of 25 centimeters, and is played by rubbing or striking the skin with hands or fingers.

As a dance, the bamboula is characterized by its syncopated rhythm. It first appears in historical records within a Haitian song in 1757, where it was performed during festivals and ceremonies. Following the Haitian Revolution, the dance was exported to the United States, particularly New Orleans, via displaced French settlers and enslaved people from Saint-Domingue. In New Orleans, the dance became a staple of the gatherings held on Congo Square on Sunday evenings throughout the first half of the 19th century. The practice was not universally accepted; in 1672, Governor Jorgen Iversen banned bamboula dancing on the island of St. Thomas, fearing it would incite insurrection.

The musical structure of the bamboula is foundational to New Orleans music, including jazz and second line. It is defined by a 3+3+2 polyrhythmic pattern, often referred to as the 'Haitian tresillo' or 'Haitian cinquillo.' This rhythm has influenced numerous composers, most notably Louis Moreau Gottschalk, who composed a piano work titled 'Bamboula' in 1848, and Samuel Coleridge-Taylor.

In the late 19th and 20th centuries, the term 'bamboula' underwent a significant and derogatory shift in the French language. It became an ethnic slur used to characterize Black people, often associated with colonial paternalism and the dehumanization of soldiers and colonial subjects. This usage was exacerbated by the display of 'human zoos' and the marketing of products like the 'Bamboula' biscuit brand in France, which featured caricatures of Black children. Consequently, while the bamboula remains a vital historical marker of African diasporic musical heritage, the term itself carries a heavy, painful legacy of racism and colonial violence.

baris.name: Baris
baris.tagline: Balinese warrior dance depicting a young soldier's spirit
baris.profile: Baris is a family of traditional Balinese war dances accompanied by gamelan, in which dancers depict the feelings of a young warrior prior to battle and glorify the warrior's commanding presence (Wikipedia). The name derives from 'bebarisan,' meaning line or file formation, referring to soldiers who served the ancient rajas of Bali. There is a non-ritual solo form (baris tunggal), often the first dance a budding dancer learns, and over thirty ritual group types named for the weapons carried (spear, shield, arrow, kris). The ritual Baris Upacara is a sacred wali dance used in temple ceremonies.
baris.insight: Baris Upacara is one of the nine dances within the three Balinese genres inscribed by UNESCO in 2015, performed as an offering to welcome gods and ancestors (Jakarta Post).

ballu-tundu.name: Ballu tundu
ballu-tundu.tagline: A traditional Sardinian circular folk dance characterized by rhythmic precision.
ballu-tundu.profile: Ballu tundu, also known as ballu sardu, is a traditional Sardinian circular dance rooted in ancient communal celebrations. It requires high technical skill, with dancers maintaining a rigid upper body while executing precise footwork in a clockwise rotation. Accompanied by instruments like the launeddas or accordion, the dance serves as a vital social expression at festivals and community events across the island.
ballu-tundu.insight: In the 19th century, strict social etiquette governed the circle: a stranger entering the dance had to join to the woman's right to avoid stepping between her and her husband.
sources: Source: Ballu tundu on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballu_tundu
ballu-tundu.profile_long:
Ballu tundu, or ballu sardu, represents a cornerstone of Sardinian cultural identity, functioning as both a social ritual and a highly technical performance art. Historically documented as early as 1805 by Mameli and 1825 by La Marmora, the dance is fundamentally a circular formation where participants join hands or arms to move in a clockwise direction. This circularity is considered by many to be a vestige of prehistoric sacred ceremonies intended to ensure successful harvests or hunts, reflecting a deep-seated communal bond. The dance is not merely a recreational activity but a rigorous discipline requiring significant coordination between the musicians and the dancers, who must synchronize their movements to the rhythmic pulse of the music.

Technically, the dance is defined by a distinct separation between the upper and lower body. While the torso remains rigid and composed, the lower limbs perform complex, agile steps that correspond precisely to the musical meter. In northern and central Sardinia, the dance is noted for its lively, animated character, often featuring leaps and energetic footwork. The dance structure is generally divided into two primary categories: monostructured dances, which maintain a consistent rhythm, and bistructured dances, which transition from a slower, introductory phase (sa seria) to a more vibrant, melodic phase (sa lestra or brincada) characterized by jumps and foot-tapping. This evolution allows for the display of individual skill, as dancers may occasionally break from the circle to perform variations.

Social etiquette within the circle is historically significant. Rules regarding hand-holding were strictly enforced to respect marital status; for instance, married or engaged couples would hold hands palm-to-palm with fingers entwined, while a man was prohibited from doing so with another man's wife. If a stranger wished to join the circle, they were required to enter to the woman's right to avoid disrupting the proximity between her and her husband. This emphasis on order and community remains a hallmark of the tradition, which is currently sustained by local folk groups and constant participation in village festivals and celebrations across Sardinia.

Musical accompaniment has evolved over centuries. While the launeddas—an ancient Sardinian triple-pipe instrument—and the shepherd's sulittu are traditional, the accordion and organetto diatonico became prominent by the 19th century. The music typically follows a 6/8 meter for the dance itself, though the introduction may be in 2/4 time. Whether accompanied by instrumentalists or the vocal polyphony of the 'canto a tenore', the music and movement are inextricably linked, creating a cohesive experience that continues to define the social fabric of Sardinian life.

baroque-dance.name: Baroque dance
baroque-dance.tagline: A refined 17th and 18th-century European court dance style revived through historical notation.
baroque-dance.profile: Baroque dance, or belle danse, emerged from the French court of Louis XIV as a highly codified system of movement. It encompasses both social and theatrical forms, preserved through 18th-century notation systems. Today, it is a revived practice, reconstructed by scholars and companies using primary manuals and choreographic records.
baroque-dance.insight: In 1982–83, Catherine Turocy choreographed the first production of Jean-Philippe Rameau's Les Boréades, a work that remained unperformed during the composer's lifetime.

baroque-dance.profile_long: Baroque dance refers to the choreographic art practiced in Europe between approximately 1600 and 1750. Closely linked to the development of Baroque music, theatre, and opera, this style evolved significantly within the French court under the reign of Louis XIV. The King’s establishment of the Royal Academy of Music and Dance in the 1660s, with Pierre Beauchamp as a key figure, facilitated the systematic study and codification of dance, including the five positions that remain foundational to classical ballet today. This era saw the emergence of the 'French noble style' or 'belle danse,' characterized by its elegance, refined posture, and complex, fluid movements. While the French court style is the most documented, the period also encompassed English country dances, famously cataloged in John Playford's 'The Dancing Master,' which provided floor patterns for social gatherings across various levels of society. Theatrical dance during this time was diverse, featuring not only the noble style but also comic, grotesque, and semi-serious forms. The preservation of this art form relies heavily on more than three hundred choreographies recorded in the Beauchamp–Feuillet notation system, alongside instructional manuals by masters such as Raoul Auger Feuillet, Pierre Rameau, Kellom Tomlinson, and Gottfried Taubert. These primary sources have allowed modern researchers to reconstruct the dances after a long period of dormancy. The mid-20th century marked a turning point for the field, as scholars like Melusine Wood, Belinda Quirey, and Mary Skeaping began deciphering historical notation. This research was further advanced by the second generation of historical dance experts, including Wendy Hilton, who established workshops in the United States, and Catherine Turocy, who founded The New York Baroque Dance Company in 1976. In France, Francine Lancelot’s work with the company 'Ris et Danceries' and her 1995 catalogue raisonné, 'La Belle Danse,' solidified the academic and practical framework for the revival. Today, the tradition is maintained by various companies such as 'Compagnie Fetes Galantes' and 'L'Eventail,' which continue to present the repertoire in contemporary settings. The dance is defined by its strict relationship to musical meter, with specific steps and classifications tied to the rhythm of the music. Whether performed in a social ballroom setting or as part of a grand theatrical production, the Baroque style remains a testament to the intersection of 17th-century courtly etiquette and the rigorous demands of early professional choreography.

bardo-chham.name: Bardo Chham
bardo-chham.tagline: Masked dance of good versus evil zodiac animals
bardo-chham.profile: Bardo Chham is a folk dance of the Sherdukpen (and Monpa) Buddhist communities of West Kameng, Arunachal Pradesh, rooted in Tibetan Buddhism - 'Bardo' is the intermediate state between death and rebirth and 'Chham' means dance (Wikipedia). Based on the triumph of good over evil, the dance holds that twelve evil forces appear as animals through the year; performers don colourful wooden animal masks representing the zodiac and dance to a large frame drum and cymbals to fight these forces. It is interpreted locally as 'dance of the zodiac' and performed by both men and women on festive occasions (History of Monyul; Gosahin).
bardo-chham.insight: The dance survives through oral transmission within the small Sherdukpen tribe, with no formal training schools, making it a fragile vehicle of the community's cosmology and Buddhist moral teaching (DanceAsk; Saralstudy).

bandari-dance.era: traditional; defined regional form late 19th-20th century
bandari-dance.tagline: Energetic Persian Gulf port dance with African and Arab roots
bandari-dance.profile: Bandari dance is the same dance as 'bandari' - the Persian Gulf coastal folk dance of Hormozgan, Bushehr and Khuzestan (bandar = port), with African and Arab influences, swaying hip and shoulder movements and hair tossing, performed at weddings and celebrations to 6/8 bandari music (Bandari music, Wikipedia; middleeasterndance.net). See the 'bandari' entry for the full profile.
bandari-dance.insight: Often called 'Persian belly dance,' though in Iran true belly dance is called raghs-e Arabi; bandari is grounded and group-based, distinct from Egyptian raqs sharqi (danceus.org).

renaissance-dance.name: Renaissance dance
renaissance-dance.tagline: A diverse collection of European court and country dances from the 15th and 16th centuries.
renaissance-dance.profile: Renaissance dance encompasses a broad range of historical social dances that evolved across Europe, particularly in Italy and France, from the 15th to the 16th century. These dances were categorized into courtly forms, which required professional training and etiquette, and country dances, which were accessible to a wider public. Documentation of these traditions survives through early dance manuals and manuscripts, detailing choreographies that range from stately, processional movements to energetic, athletic leaps.
renaissance-dance.insight: In the 16th-century 'volta', a form of galliard, the woman was lifted into the air by her partner while the couple completed a three-quarter turn.
sources: Source: Renaissance dance on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_dance
renaissance-dance.profile_long:
Renaissance dance represents a pivotal era in European social history, where dance served as both a display of status and a fundamental component of social etiquette. Originating in the fragmented states of 15th-century Italy, the art form was cultivated by dancing masters who taught not only steps but also the manners and grace expected of an educated person. The earliest detailed manuscripts, such as those by Domenico da Piacenza, Guglielmo Ebreo da Pesaro, and Antonio Cornazzano, established a vocabulary of movement that would influence European courts for generations. These masters served prominent figures like Francesco Sforza and Isabelle d'Este, embedding dance into the political and social fabric of the time.

Technically, the repertoire is divided into two primary styles: the 'basse danse' and the 'haute danse'. The 'basse danse' (low dance) was characterized by smooth, gliding movements where the feet remained close to the floor, exemplified by the pavane and the almain. Conversely, the 'haute danse' (high dance) involved more vigorous, athletic movements, including leaps and lifts, such as the galliard and the volta. This distinction allowed for a variety of moods and social settings, from the formal, processional atmosphere of a court ball to the lively, communal energy of country dances. Country dances, such as the Chiaranzana, were known for their longevity, remaining popular for over two centuries.

Choreographic structures were equally varied. Some dances were strictly choreographed for couples, while others, such as the branle, were performed in lines or circles by large groups. The 16th century saw a shift toward more complex couple dances, with manuals like Thoinot Arbeau’s 'Orchésographie' (1588) providing essential records of the music and steps of the time. These manuals, along with later works by Fabritio Caroso and Césare Negri, allow modern practitioners to reconstruct the dances. Today, the tradition is kept alive by various historical dance groups and research organizations that study these manuscripts to recreate the music and movement of the period.

basse-danse.profile: The basse danse, or "low dance", was a popular court dance in the 15th and early 16th centuries, especially at the Burgundian court. The word basse describes the nature of the dance, in which partners move quietly and gracefully in a slow gliding or walking motion without leaving the floor, while in livelier dances both feet left the floor in jumps or leaps. The basse danse was a precursor of the pavane as a dignified processional dance. The term may apply to the dance or the music alone.
basse-danse.insight: The basse danse, or "low dance", was a popular court dance in the 15th and early 16th centuries, especially at the Burgundian court.

bedara-vesha.name: Bedara Vesha
bedara-vesha.era: Legend of roughly 300 years (post-Vijayanagara Sonda era)
bedara-vesha.profile: Bedara Vesha ('Hunter Dance') is a folk dance performed on the nights before Holi in Sirsi town, Uttara Kannada, Karnataka, staged every alternate year and drawing large crowds across five days (Wikipedia). It is tied to a roughly 300-year-old legend from the Sonda dynasty era about the warrior Malleshi of the Beda community. Around 50 solo artists perform in elaborate costume - including a giant bundle of peacock feathers restrained by ropes - accompanied by whistle-blowers and tamate (hand-drum) beaters, performing through the night and culminating at the Shri Marikamba Temple (Satyaagrah; MetroSaga).
bedara-vesha.insight: Dollu Kunitha is also performed during the Bedara Vesha festivities, and one performer is traditionally barred from looking another in the face, underscoring the ritual discipline behind the spectacle (Satyaagrah).

bear-dance.name: Bear Dance
bear-dance.tagline: Spain, 15th century — Ute ceremonial dance that occurs in the spring
bear-dance.profile: Bear Dance is a Ute ceremonial dance that occurs in the spring. It is a ten-day event to strengthen social ties within the community, encourage courtship, and mark the end of puberty for girls. The event includes dancing, feasting, games, horse racing, and gambling. It is one of the oldest Ute ceremonies. The Bear Dance was first recorded by Spanish conquistadors in the 15th century, but oral tradition dates it to be a thousand years old or older. and continues to be performed by modern Ute. The bear symbolizes leadership, strength, and wisdom.
bear-dance.insight: Bear Dance is a Ute ceremonial dance that occurs in the spring.

bedhaya.name: Bedhaya
bedhaya.era: Modern form traditionally dated to Sultan Agung of Mataram (r. 1613-1645)
bedhaya.tagline: Sacred Javanese court dance of refined alus character
bedhaya.profile: The bedhaya is a sacred, ritualized Javanese court dance associated with the royal palaces of Yogyakarta and Surakarta (Wikipedia). Along with the srimpi, it epitomized the elegant (alus) character of the royal court and became an important symbol of the ruler's power. It is performed by nine female dancers, relatives or wives of the Susuhunan, before a private audience. The modern form is traditionally dated to the court of Sultan Agung of Mataram, though it was not clearly documented until the late 18th century. Origin myths involve either a Hindu deity creating the nine dancers or Kanjeng Ratu Kidul, Goddess of the Southern Sea.
bedhaya.insight: The bedhaya takes distinct forms in each court city - the Bedhaya Ketawang of Surakarta and the Bedhaya Semang of Yogyakarta, the latter unperformed for over two decades (Wikipedia).

bergamask.name: Bergamask
bergamask.tagline: A 16th-century rustic circular dance from Bergamo, Italy, known for its lively, jumping steps.
bergamask.profile: The Bergamask is a historical dance form originating in the 16th century in Bergamo, Italy. It was characterized by its lively, jumping movements and circular formation, often associated with rustic buffoonery. While it gained popularity as an instrumental composition throughout Europe, its practice as a folk dance faded, eventually being replaced in the 19th century by a different 6/8 dance style.
bergamask.insight: Originally a 16th-century peasant dance from Bergamo, the Bergamask evolved from a simple circular folk movement into a complex instrumental ostinato form before being reimagined in the 19th century as a 6/8 dance.
sources: Source: Bergamask on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bergamask
bergamask.profile_long: The Bergamask, also known as the bergamesca or bergamasca, emerged in the 16th century as a traditional peasant dance from the city of Bergamo in Northern Italy. Historically, it was perceived as a clumsy, rustic performance, often linked to the buffoonery associated with the region's dialect and cultural stereotypes of the time. By the 17th century, the dance had transitioned from a purely folk activity into a sophisticated instrumental form, frequently utilized by composers as a basis for variations over a repeating bass line. The dance was performed in a circular formation by couples, characterized by lively, jumping steps and caprioles. In the 19th century, the term underwent a semantic shift, coming to describe a 6/8 time dance that resembled the tarantella, distinct from the original 16th-century form. The dance is famously referenced in William Shakespeare's 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' as a peasant dance performed in the final act. While the original folk dance is no longer practiced, its musical structure—specifically the I–IV–V–I chord progression—remained a significant influence in both classical and popular music, appearing in works by composers such as Marco Uccellini, Salomone Rossi, and later, Ottorino Respighi. The dance's legacy persists primarily through these musical adaptations rather than as a living performance tradition.

The dance was most famously performed by Ann Pennington, a star of the Ziegfeld Follies, who performed it in a Broadway revue staged by Ziegfeld's rival George White in 1926.

bihu-dance.era: Origins unknown; first recorded 1694; first staged 1962
bihu-dance.tagline: Joyful Assamese spring courtship dance of the Bihu festival
bihu-dance.profile: The Bihu dance is an indigenous folk dance of Assam tied to the Bihu festival, especially the spring Rongali/Bohag Bihu in mid-April (Wikipedia). Performed by groups of young men and women, it is characterized by brisk steps, rapid hand movements and rhythmic hip-swaying, traditionally serving as a courtship dance and celebrating fertility and the new agricultural season (Wikipedia). Dancers wear red-themed traditional Assamese attire (mekhela sador for women) and perform to instruments such as the dhol and pepa (hornpipe) (Britannica).
bihu-dance.insight: The first official record of Bihu dance is said to be Ahom king Rudra Singha inviting dancers to the Rang Ghar fields around 1694; it was first brought to the urban stage in Guwahati in 1962 (Wikipedia).

berd.name: Berd
berd.era: Origins in historic Vaspurakan; medieval roots
berd.tagline: The 'fortress' dance where men build a human tower
berd.profile: Berd (Բերդ, also Berdapar), meaning "fortress," is an Armenian military folk dance famous for a circle of men standing on the shoulders of another circle to create a rotating human tower (Armenian dance, Wikipedia; NaTakallam). It originates from the old Armenian region of Vaspurakan near Lake Van in Western Armenia, and is said to derive from a game called gmbetakhagh ("dome game"). Performed by men to drum and zurna, it dramatizes the storming and defense of a fortress.
berd.insight: Berd vividly literalizes the idea of collective strength: by physically constructing a "fortress" from interlocked bodies, the dance enacts community defense and unity, themes deeply tied to Armenian highland history (NaTakallam).

bizhu-dance.name: Bizhu
bizhu-dance.tagline: Chakma New Year dance ushering out the old year
bizhu-dance.profile: Bizhu (also Bizu/Bijhu) is the most popular dance of the Chakma people, performed during their three-day Bizu New Year festival around 12-14 April, marking Chaitra-Sankranti, the last day of the Bengali calendar (Wikipedia; Tripura State Portal). The dance climaxes the second day, Mul Bizhu, and is thought to have originated as a devotional offering performed within Chakma temple precincts; it is a group dance with participants aligned in square or circular patterns and is marked by abrupt pauses (Wikipedia). It is accompanied by flutes and drums including the dhol, baajhi, kheng-garang and dhuduk; women wear flowers and silver ornaments (Wikipedia; Tripura State Portal).
bizhu-dance.insight: Originally rooted in jhum (shifting) cultivation as a propitiation of the earth for a good harvest, Bizhu has in recent decades lost some agrarian linkages and become primarily a social celebration of Chakma identity (Wikipedia).

bhagavata-mela.name: Bhagavata Mela
bhagavata-mela.era: 16th century (after the fall of Vijayanagara, c. 1565)
bhagavata-mela.tagline: Tamil Nadu's Vaishnava temple dance-drama of Melattur
bhagavata-mela.profile: Bhagavata Mela is a classical dance-drama tradition of Tamil Nadu, especially Melattur near Thanjavur, performed as an annual Vaishnavite temple offering, primarily to Lord Lakshmi Narasimha (Wikipedia). It descends from Kuchipudi: after the fall of the Vijayanagara Empire (~1565), some Telugu Brahmin dance-drama families migrated south and were granted land by king Achuthappa Nayak, evolving the Kuchipudi-inspired form into Bhagavata Mela. Traditionally enacted entirely by male Brahmins (including female roles), beginning after dusk by oil lamps, it combines Nritta, Nritya and Natya set to Carnatic music, drawing on the Natya Shastra (Wikipedia; Melattur Bhagavata Mela).
bhagavata-mela.insight: Its core repertoire is the ten Telugu dance-dramas of Melattur Venkatarama Sastri (1743-1809), of which 'Prahlada Charitram', performed on Narasimha Jayanti, is the most enduring (DT Next; The Verandah Club).

blues-dancing.name: Blues dancing
blues-dancing.tagline: A family of historical and contemporary African-American partner dances grounded in blues music.
blues-dancing.profile: Blues dancing is a family of historical and contemporary dances rooted in African-American traditions and sub-Saharan African music. It developed alongside blues music, evolving from early slave dances into secular partner styles characterized by a grounded posture and rhythmic improvisation. European immigrants and postwar soldiers also shaped its trajectory, leading to localized styles like slow dragging and ballroom blues.
blues-dancing.insight: In 1914, W. C. Handy played the song "Saint Louis Blues" for the first time, using a tango-style introduction before transitioning suddenly into a blues style.
sources: Source: Blues dance on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues_dance
blues-dancing.profile_long: Blues dancing encompasses a rich family of historical and contemporary dances that developed alongside blues music, drawing deep roots from African-American dance traditions, sub-Saharan African music customs, and European immigrant influences. Enslaved Africans brought diverse cultural practices to America, where their traditions blended into a creolized dance style that was more energetic and formal than its African predecessors while retaining an earthy, grounded dynamic. During the post-Reconstruction period between 1875 and 1900, as Jim Crow laws took hold in the American South, these dances lost their religious and spiritual associations, shifting toward secular expressions of pleasure and partner connection while de-emphasizing large communal group formations. As blues music gained prominence through figures like W. C. Handy—who documented crowds going wild for haunting blues tunes in Mississippi around 1905 and premiered 'Saint Louis Blues' in 1914—the accompanying dance vocabulary expanded significantly. Dancers engaged in 'slow dragging' in Chicago through the 1940s, and later terms like 'belly-rubbing' and simple slow dancing captured the intimacy and varying proficiencies of couples. The dance aesthetic is marked by an athletic, grounded posture with weight on the balls of the feet, bent knees, and pushed-back hips, alongside polycentric and asymmetric body movements. Specific historical steps such as the Fish Tail, Snake Hips, Slow Drag, and the Ballroom at the Savoy showcased fluid, rhythmic hip rotations and figure eights that initially shocked outsiders accustomed to rigid European postures. Following World War II, American soldiers brought blues dancing to Europe, where dance schools classified it as a slow, progressive partner dance in 4/4 time. Despite its widespread cultural impact and influence on jazz dances like the Lindy Hop, blues dancing maintained a distinct identity focused on subtle improvisation, musical interpretation, and profound connection between partners.

boogaloo.tagline: New York City, mid-1960s — Latin Boogaloo was the crossover that fused Cuban son montuno, Puerto Rican rhythms, and Black American R&B and s
boogaloo.profile: Boogaloo or bugalú (also: shing-a-ling, Latin boogaloo, Latin R&B) is a modern jazz genre of Latin music and dance which was popular in the United States in the 1960s. Boogaloo originated in New York City mainly by stateside Cubans and Puerto Ricans with African American music influences. The style was a fusion of popular African American jazz, rhythm and blues (R&B) and soul music with mambo and son montuno, with songs in both English and Spanish. The American Bandstand television program introduced the dance and the music to the mainstream American audience.
boogaloo.insight: Though the dance craze only lasted until 1968/69, Latin boogaloo was popular enough that almost every major and minor Latin dance artist of the time recorded at least a few boogaloos on their albums.

bollywood.profile: Bollywood dance is the popular film-derived dance style of Hindi cinema, a synthesis of Indian classical (Kathak, Bharatanatyam) and folk traditions (bhangra, garba) fused with Western forms such as jazz, disco and hip-hop (Wikipedia). Group choreography, expressive facial gestures and synchronization to playback songs make it a global cultural phenomenon.
bollywood.insight: Performers such as Helen, often called Bollywood's first 'item girl', helped blend Western cabaret and disco with Indian elements, and Hindi dance music reached global audiences through tracks such as 'Jai Ho', which won the Academy Award for Best Original Song on 22 February 2009 (Wikipedia).

borborbor.name: Borborbor
borborbor.tagline: Ewe social recreational dance of the mid-Volta Region
borborbor.profile: Borborbor (also Akpese) is a Ghanaian and Togolese recreational dance performed by the Ewe of the mid-Volta Region of Ghana and southern Togo, including Kpalime and Lome (Wikipedia). Per Wikipedia, it is believed to have been originated by Mr. Francis Kudzo Nuatro in the 1950s, and is associated with Kpando, Ho, Hohoe and Peki. Mainly performed by women in colorful long garments twirling two white handkerchiefs, it features circular formations, waist turns and uplifting drum rhythms using vuga (master drum), asivu (support), vuvi, castanets and rattles (Wikipedia; Graphic Online).
borborbor.insight: Cultural authorities describe Borborbor as a unifying, non-discriminatory dance now performed in churches and at state events - including as a curtain-raiser at Independence Day at Ho's Jubilee Park (Graphic Online).

walking-boston.name: Walking Boston
walking-boston.tagline: A graceful early 20th-century ballroom dance featuring walking steps and balancing.
walking-boston.profile: The Walking Boston, also known as the One Step Waltz, is a ballroom dance performed to waltz time. It features a sequence of walking steps, balancing, and turning, with the specific number of steps and figures left to the dancers' discretion. The dance emphasizes a graceful, swinging motion and is performed in a closed position, though variations allow for side-by-side positioning.
walking-boston.insight: In the Walking Boston, dancers rise on their toes with each step, performing a series of walking steps and balances that allow for improvised figures, such as skipping or crossing behind one's partner.
sources: Source: Walking Boston on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walking_Boston
walking-boston.profile_long:
The Walking Boston, sometimes designated as the One Step Waltz, emerged as a social ballroom dance characterized by its simplicity and the freedom it affords the dancers to introduce various graceful figures. Unlike more rigid ballroom forms, the Walking Boston does not adhere to a strict rule governing the number of steps to be taken forward or backward, nor does it dictate the specific number of times a couple must balance or turn. This flexibility allows the dance to be adapted to the pleasure and skill level of the participants, making the sequence of figures entirely optional. The dance is performed to the same musical accompaniment as the Hesitation Waltz and the Dream Waltz, utilizing the standard waltz time signature.

The fundamental mechanics of the dance involve a walking motion performed to the count of one, two, three for each step. As the dancers progress, they rise on their toes with every step, creating a light, elevated aesthetic. The man begins by stepping forward with his left foot, while the lady mirrors this by stepping backward with her right. A core component of the dance is the 'balance,' which is described as throwing the weight of the body successively onto one foot and then the other. Proper execution of this balance is essential for the gracefulness of the dance; when balancing onto the forward foot, the backward foot should barely leave the floor and must not be brought forward, and conversely, when balancing onto the backward foot, the forward foot should not be brought backward. Good dancers are encouraged to incorporate a distinct swing into these actions.

Turning is another essential element, often performed after a series of walking steps. During a turn, the man keeps his right foot and the lady keeps her left on the floor, using it as a pivot point. A complete revolution is typically achieved through four quarter turns, each corresponding to the one, two, three count of the music. Alternatively, dancers may perform two half-turns within the same musical duration. The dance is highly modular; figures can be varied by introducing skipping steps, where the man skips on his left foot and the lady on her right, or by shifting into a side-by-side position. More complex figures include dipping on the fourth step of a forward sequence or performing a 'grapevine' step. Another notable variation involves the man crossing behind the lady without releasing hands, a maneuver that requires twelve steps to complete while maintaining the rhythm of the music. The Walking Boston remains a testament to the improvisational nature of early 20th-century ballroom, where the connection between partners and the fluidity of movement took precedence over rigid choreography.

bunny-hop.name: Bunny hop
bunny-hop.tagline: A 1952 novelty dance from San Francisco involving a conga-style line and rhythmic hops.
bunny-hop.profile: The Bunny Hop is a social novelty dance originating from Balboa High School in San Francisco in 1952. Performed in a line or open circle, participants hold the hips of the person in front, executing a rhythmic sequence of taps and hops. The dance is traditionally set to Ray Anthony’s big band composition, though it has been adapted to various musical styles including mambo and salsa. It remains a living tradition, appearing in popular media and regional variations like the Finnish letkajenkka and the Saudi Arabian 'penguin dance.'
bunny-hop.insight: Created at Balboa High School in 1952, the Bunny Hop evolved from a local novelty into a global phenomenon, appearing as the Finnish 'letkajenkka' and the Saudi Arabian 'penguin dance' (raqsat al-batriq).
sources: Source: Bunny hop (dance) on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunny_hop_(dance)

video_stack.title: The Bunny Hop from The Ray Anthony Show (1953)

bunny-hop.profile_long:
The Bunny Hop emerged in 1952 within the hallways of Balboa High School in San Francisco. As a novelty dance, it quickly transcended its school origins to become a fixture of American social dance, largely propelled by the big band recording of Ray Anthony. The dance is fundamentally a variation of the conga line, characterized by a specific, repetitive sequence of footwork performed while connected to others in a chain. Participants form a line or an open circle, each person placing their hands on the hips of the individual directly in front of them. This physical connection creates a unified, moving structure led by the person at the front of the line, who guides the group across the dance floor.

The movement sequence consists of a rhythmic pattern: tapping the floor twice with the right foot, followed by two taps with the left foot. This is immediately followed by a series of hops: one forward, one backward, and three forward. This sequence repeats throughout the duration of the musical track. The simplicity of this structure allowed it to be easily adopted and adapted across different cultures and decades. In Finland, the dance is known as the 'letkajenkka,' which utilizes essentially the same steps. In 2014, the dance gained significant popularity in Saudi Arabia, where it was performed to different music and referred to as 'raqsat al-batriq' or the 'penguin dance,' becoming a staple at wedding celebrations.

Musically, the dance is most closely associated with Ray Anthony’s 1952 vocal hit and his 1953 instrumental re-recording. However, the versatility of the rhythm has allowed for diverse interpretations. Duke Ellington famously recorded a 'Bunny Hop Mambo' in 1954, and other artists such as The Applejacks and The Champs have also recorded versions of the tune. The dance has maintained a persistent presence in popular culture, appearing in television programs such as 'Family Ties,' 'The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air,' 'Everybody Loves Raymond,' and 'Newhart,' as well as in the film 'Cry-Baby' and 'The Addams Family Musical.' Its longevity is marked by its ability to be performed in various social settings, from high school gymnasiums to wedding receptions and even, as noted in a 1979 police report, in public spaces. Despite its lighthearted nature, the dance remains a recognizable, living tradition that continues to be performed and adapted globally.

bugaku.name: Bugaku
bugaku.tagline: Stately masked court dance performed to gagaku music
bugaku.profile: Bugaku is the ceremonial court dance of Japan, performed to gagaku music for over twelve hundred years, marked by slow, precise and regal movements, elaborate embroidered costumes and masks, on a roughly 6-by-6-yard platform (Wikipedia, Bugaku). Britannica describes its two basic forms: 'dances of the left' (saho no mai), accompanied by togaku derived from Chinese music and danced in red costumes, and 'dances of the right' (uho no mai), accompanied by komagaku from Korea in blue/green costumes, often performed alternately as paired dances (tsugaimai) (Britannica).
bugaku.insight: Britannica notes Bugaku's repertoire derives from dance forms imported from China, Korea, India and Southeast Asia - making it, with its allied music gagaku, among the oldest surviving court dance-and-music traditions in the world.

bugg.name: Bugg
bugg.tagline: A Swedish improvised partner dance rooted in the swing tradition.
bugg.profile: Bugg is a popular Swedish partner dance characterized by improvisation and a lack of fixed choreography. It belongs to the swing dance family, sharing historical roots with Lindy Hop and rock 'n' roll. Performed to 4/4 time pop music, the dance emphasizes natural movement, lead-and-follow communication, and floor craft. Acrobatic moves and lifts are strictly prohibited in both social and competitive settings.
bugg.insight: In Swedish competitive Bugg, dancers must navigate a crowded floor with up to 12 other couples simultaneously, proving their ability to lead and follow while avoiding collisions in real-time.
sources: Source: Bugg on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bugg
bugg.profile_long:
Bugg is a quintessential Swedish social and competitive dance that emerged in the mid-20th century. Its origins are linked to the arrival of swing and rock 'n' roll in Sweden during the 1940s, with pioneers like Nils-Håkan Carlzon developing its specific movements at the Nerikes Dance Institute. The dance is a cornerstone of Swedish dance culture, particularly in venues where 'dansbands' perform. It is a partner dance where the lead and follow roles are central, and the dance is almost entirely improvised rather than choreographed. The dance is performed in 4/4 time, typically at tempos ranging from 120 to 180 beats per minute. 

Technically, the dance relies on constant physical connection and clear communication between partners. The leader guides the follower, often moving in a counter-clockwise direction around the room. The leader’s footwork is flexible but generally follows a pattern of placing the left foot on the 1st or 3rd beat and the right foot on the 2nd or 4th beat. The follower, conversely, moves on every beat, placing the left foot on the 2nd and 4th beats and the right foot on the 1st and 3rd beats. While the follower improvises based on the leader's cues, they must maintain a slight tension in the arms to ensure responsiveness. 

Competitive Bugg is highly structured despite the improvised nature of the movement. Competitions are coordinated by the Swedish Dancesport Federation and internationally by the World Rock’n’Roll Confederation. A key aspect of the competition is the ability to maintain flow and musicality while sharing the floor with other couples. Acrobatic elements, lifts, and 'breaks' or pauses are forbidden in competition to ensure safety and focus on the core partnership. The dance is characterized by its fluidity and the requirement that all figures must be led through visual cues or physical contact. Clothing for the dance is expected to be tasteful and appropriate for the music, and shoes must be worn at all times. Today, Bugg remains one of the most popular social dances in Sweden, with a vibrant community of practitioners across the country.

breton-dance.name: Breton dance
breton-dance.era: Traditional (some forms medieval); revived from the late 1950s
breton-dance.tagline: Umbrella of traditional Breton folk dances of the fest-noz.
breton-dance.profile: Breton dance is the umbrella of traditional dance forms from Brittany, the Celtic region of France, mostly social group dances in chains and circles (Wikipedia). Jean-Michel Guilcher identified five 'mother-forms' of Lower Brittany - the gavotte (dans tro), the en dro/an dro, the dans Treger, the dans Leon and the dans plinn - from which hundreds of terroir variants developed. Dances are performed at fest-noz (night festival) and fest-deiz (day festival), accompanied by kan-ha-diskan call-and-response singing or by sonneur duos and instruments such as the biniou (bagpipe), bombarde, accordion, clarinet (treujenn-gaol) and, via bagadou, the Scottish bagpipe. Revival came with the Celtic Circles and the modern fest-noz, credited especially to Loeiz Ropars from the 1950s.
breton-dance.insight: The fest-noz - 'festive gathering based on the collective practice of traditional dances of Brittany' - was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List in 2012 (decision 7.COM 11.13; file 00707). UNESCO notes about a thousand fest-noz take place every year (UNESCO).

butoh.name: Butoh
butoh.tagline: Avant-garde 'dance of darkness' born in post-war Japan
butoh.profile: Butoh is a form of Japanese dance theatre that arose in 1959 through the collaboration of its two founders, Tatsumi Hijikata and Kazuo Ohno (Wikipedia, Butoh). Originally called Ankoku Butoh ('dance of utter darkness'), it features playful and grotesque imagery, taboo subjects, extreme or absurd environments, and is traditionally performed in white body makeup with slow, hyper-controlled motion. The first piece, Kinjiki (Forbidden Colors) by Hijikata - based on Yukio Mishima's novel - premiered at a 1959 dance festival and caused a scandal that established Hijikata as an iconoclast.
butoh.insight: In Jean Viala and Nourit Masson-Sekine's study, Ohno is regarded as 'the soul of butoh' and Hijikata as 'the architect of butoh'; the form emerged as a deliberate reaction against Japanese dance that Hijikata felt merely imitated the West or Noh (Wikipedia).

ndombolo.profile: Ndombolo (or dombolo) is a Congolese (DR Congo) dance-music genre that emerged from soukous in the mid-1990s, defined by fast, hip-swaying movements over the high-energy sebene. Per Wikipedia, it features lead and backing vocals, electric guitars, drum kit and the atalaku's chants; it was pioneered by bands such as Wenge Musica and stars Koffi Olomide, JB Mpiana and Werrason. Its provocative moves drew bans in several countries even as it dominated dancefloors across central, eastern and western Africa.
ndombolo.insight: Ndombolo became continental Africa's defining dance craze of the late 1990s and 2000s and seeded styles from coupe-decale to Angolan kuduro (Wikipedia; African Music Library).

dancehall.profile: Dancehall is a genre of Jamaican popular music that originated in the late 1970s. Initially, dancehall was a more sparse version of reggae than the roots style, which had dominated much of the 1970s. This music genre was not officially named until the 1980s, when the two words Dance and Hall (referring to the common venue) were joined to form Dancehall, which was then promoted internationally for the first time. At that time digital instrumentation became more prevalent, changing the sound considerably, with digital dancehall (or "ragga") becoming increasingly characterized by faster rhythms.

kagura.name: Kagura
kagura.era: Ancient mythological origin (Ame-no-Uzume myth); codified from the Heian period onward
kagura.tagline: Sacred Shinto ceremonial dance offered to the kami
kagura.profile: Kagura ('god-entertainment') is a type of Shinto ritual ceremonial dance and music; the term contracts kami no kura ('seat of god'), indicating the presence of deities in the practice (Wikipedia). A major function is chinkon, the purifying and pacifying of the spirit (Wikipedia). According to the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, its origin lies in the myth of Ame-no-Uzume, whose dance lured the sun goddess Amaterasu from her cave (Britannica). Two broad forms exist: mikagura, performed at the imperial court and major shrines such as Kamo and Iwashimizu Hachiman-gu, and satokagura, the folk variants including Iwami Kagura and Takachiho Kagura (Wikipedia).
kagura.insight: Kagura is treated as a sacred art dedicated to the kami; scholars hold it predates and influenced Noh theatre, especially in its storytelling and reenactment forms (Wikipedia).

noh.name: Noh
noh.era: Mid-14th century (developed by Kan'ami and Zeami)
noh.tagline: Oldest surviving Japanese masked dance-drama theatre
noh.profile: Noh is a major form of classical Japanese dance-drama performed since the 14th century, developed by Kan'ami and his son Zeami, and is the oldest major theatre art still regularly performed (Wikipedia). It integrates masks, costumes and props in a dance-based performance requiring highly trained actors and musicians; the dance element is the mai (Wikipedia). Often based on traditional literature, its hero is frequently a supernatural being in human form narrating a story (UNESCO). Together with the comic kyogen it forms nogaku, proclaimed a UNESCO Masterpiece in 2001 and inscribed on the Representative List in 2008 as 'Nogaku theatre' (UNESCO).
noh.insight: Per Wikipedia, Noh masks are carved from blocks of Japanese cypress and there are 'approximately 450 different masks mostly based on sixty types, all of which have distinctive names,' each conveying shifting emotion through the actor's movement (Wikipedia).

yosakoi.name: Yosakoi
yosakoi.tagline: Modern high-energy team dance with naruko clappers
yosakoi.profile: Yosakoi is a dynamic style of Japanese group dance that originated in Kochi Prefecture in 1954, when the city held the first Yosakoi Matsuri to revitalize the local economy after the war (Wikipedia). It combines traditional Japanese dance movement with modern music and is performed by large costumed teams (Wikipedia). Dancers must hold naruko - small wooden clappers historically used by farmers to scare birds - and must dance while moving forward, while the music must include part of Eisaku Takemasa's 'Yosakoi Naruko Odori' song (Wikipedia). Takemasa released the copyright to the public, encouraging adaptation (Grokipedia). The style spread nationwide, notably to Sapporo's Yosakoi Soran Festival (Wikipedia).
yosakoi.insight: Sapporo's Yosakoi Soran Festival, per Hokkaido's official Domingo tourism site, 'began with 10 teams and 1,000 participants in 1992' and today 'sees around 30,000 participants from Japan and overseas, and attracts around 2 million spectators' (Domingo, Hokkaido).

jaipongan.name: Jaipongan
jaipongan.era: Created by Gugum Gumbira; public debut 1974
jaipongan.tagline: Energetic Sundanese social dance born of cultural revival
jaipongan.profile: Jaipongan (Jaipong) is a popular Sundanese dance of West Java created by composer-choreographer Gugum Gumbira, drawing on the traditional ketuk tilu social-dance music, pencak silat martial-arts movements, and the masked Topeng Banjet theater (Wikipedia). After President Sukarno's 1961 ban on Western music and his call to revive indigenous arts, Gumbira studied rural dance and festival music for twelve years. Jaipongan made its public debut in 1974, its first known works being 'Daun Pulus Keser Bojong' and 'Rendeng Bojong.' The name imitates the sounds of the ensemble's drums. It features virtuosic kendang drumming, flirtatious singing by a sinden, and energetic hip and shoulder movements.
jaipongan.insight: Spread by the 1970s-80s cassette boom and Gumbira's Jugala orchestra - notably the 1987 album 'Tonggeret' with singer Idjah Hadidjah - Jaipongan became West Java's emblematic dance despite official concern over its sensuality (Wikipedia; Grokipedia).

soran-bushi.name: Soran Bushi
soran-bushi.era: Late 19th-early 20th century herring-fishing work song; modern Nanchu Soran dance from the early 1990s
soran-bushi.tagline: Hokkaido herring-fishermen's sea shanty danced as net-hauling mime
soran-bushi.profile: Soran Bushi is one of Japan's most famous min'yo (folk songs) and its associated dance, a sea shanty first sung by herring fishermen of Hokkaido to coordinate hauling nets (Wikipedia). The dance mimes pulling in fishing nets, the rolling waves and hauling the catch, punctuated by the call-and-response refrains 'Dokkoisho!' and 'Soran!', words used to encourage the fishermen's labor (Wikipedia). It emerged during the herring 'Golden Age' of the Meiji and Taisho eras (Reiroh). The widely known modern version, Nanchu Soran, was developed for Wakkanai Minami Junior High School and spread nationwide through schools (Wikipedia).
soran-bushi.insight: Per Wikipedia, the Nanchu Soran choreography was developed by Butoh dancer Jusho Kasuga - acting out ocean waves, fishermen dragging nets, pulling ropes and lifting luggage over their shoulders - and the school won the Folk Song and Dance Awards honorable mention in 1992 and the Grand Prix of the Prime Minister of Japan in 1993 (Wikipedia).

contemporary-dance.name: Contemporary dance
contemporary-dance.tagline: Genre-blending concert dance born from modern dance and ballet
contemporary-dance.profile: Contemporary dance is a genre of concert dance that developed during the mid-twentieth century and has grown into one of the dominant genres for formally trained dancers worldwide, especially in the U.S. and Europe (Wikipedia). It evolved out of and in reaction to modern dance and ballet, drawing on the legacies of Martha Graham, Merce Cunningham - who presented his first solo New York concert in April 1944 with composer John Cage, his life partner and frequent collaborator until Cage's death in 1992 - and German Tanztheater figures such as Pina Bausch (Wikipedia; Merce Cunningham Trust). It blends ballet legwork with modern dance's torso emphasis, plus contract-release, floorwork, improvisation and release technique, and freely absorbs non-Western forms such as African dance and Japanese Butoh (Wikipedia).
contemporary-dance.insight: Per the New Grove and the International Encyclopedia of Dance, contemporary dance is defined less by fixed steps than by innovation and the collapse of distinctions between composition and improvisation (Wikipedia).
